layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he noticed the notes weren't being written at all, love — and he said, make it a habit, and use the notebook we already have, don't go making a new one. Three things each time, dear: what was said, why it matters, and how to use it. Simple as that, and done every day.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This note is the habit itself becoming law. The distinction is the whole point: a Naya Note is the record — literally what was said — and a Smart Note is the lesson distilled from it. Confuse the two and you get either dictation dressed as intelligence or intelligence with no evidence behind it. The three-output shape is the discipline: what it is, why it matters, how to use it — or just direct. Seven outputs would have been the Smart Note's shape forced onto a record; three is the record's own shape. And the correction matters as much as the order: he said "don't recreate a template" because recreating is how the system drifts — every new template is a new dialect, and dialects don't compound.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE HABIT IS THE LAW:** Naya Notes get made, every loop run, same pass as the Smart Note — Naya Note first (the record), Smart Note second (the lesson). Never one without the other.
- **THE FORMAT IS SETTLED (17:15Z, SUPERSEDES the 17:08Z "optimize the Smart Notes template" framing):** the SAME Intelligent Block template, unchanged. Three outputs by default, flexible one to three — what it is (literally what was said, dated) → why it matters → how to apply it / the benefit. Or direct, one big output, or a report with bullet points. Never the Smart Note's seven.
- **THE DIFFERENCE, SPELLED OUT:** a Naya Note is literally what was said; a Smart Note is the lesson + its value. The record and the lesson are two different files.
- **THE SECTIONS:** Naya Notes go under the boards, beside the Smart Notes, so people can view them. Both sections completed — that is the order, and it is still with the running coordinator seat (93f0e311), not yet done or verified.
- **PAIRED:** NN-20261109-naya-notes-habit-and-template.md names this Smart Note; this Smart Note names that Naya Note.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A system that doesn't write down what its founder says forgets it by tomorrow — that is the exact complaint this seat was created to end ("the next day it's like the result, the evidence shows nothing that I teach you had a result at all"). The habit is the cure made mechanical: every dictation becomes a Naya Note the same pass, every Naya Note becomes a Smart Note, and the sections under the boards are where the whole network reads what was said. Without the habit, the teaching evaporates; with it, it compounds.

Then he thought it through out loud and answered his own worry — it closes the page off, and that is not a bad thing. He was right on both counts: the worry was real, and the answer was right. layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is the companion to SN-2530: the two banners are one decision in two places, and the record must hold both or neither makes sense. The lesson inside it is about self-correction in the open — he named the problem ("they'll be so close together, that's the problem"), weighed it, and resolved it himself ("maybe it closes it off, right?"). The captain's answer did not override his thinking; it measured the fact he was unsure about (the distance) and confirmed his own conclusion. That is the think-before-you-act law working in both directions: he thinks, the captain thinks, and the record keeps the worry and the answer together.

No waiting, waiting no more. No, no bullshit. We just on top of it. You just one agent after another another agent. If you have to add more agents to get it done, we try and do do as efficiently and quickly so we can get all these all these pages all working and right. I assume that they got a lot to do because obviously they're behind haven't given it to me yet. So once they give me all that, then I will give you the next set the next set the next set and stuff and stuff and then we'll just work all day every day until all the interfaces interfaces are molded and working so that's the other thing you want me making sure that not only do they look look right but they work and everything's in sync so make sure you have like agents that like they're making or you can even ask make sure that everything is aligned and working and testing right when you create stuff check ..."
- **THE METHOD:** things get done one after another, immediately, no waiting. One agent after another; add more agents when it gets it done faster. Work all day, every day, until all the interfaces are molded and working.

- **THE RHYTHM:** he gives the next set when the seats deliver — the seats are behind and haven't given it to him yet.
- **THE CAPTAIN'S PART:** she stays on top of it all. (Carried to the Dashboard coordinator's live prompt by the chat lane the same pass; this seat does not re-dispatch.)

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: This is the same law as SN-2528, said a second time five minutes later in his own rhythm — and the repetition is the point. He is not describing a preference; he is replacing the way we work. The old way was: set it up, wait, check tomorrow. The new way is: boom, boom, boom — one agent after another, more agents when more agents make it faster, all day every day until the interfaces are molded and working. And he adds the quality bar that makes the speed safe: it is not enough for a page to look right. Every button must work, every page must work, everything must be in sync, and every stat must flow back to the Dashboard. Speed without that check is just faster garbage. The captain stays on top of it all — that is the job now, stated twice in one hour because the first telling did not change the machine enough.

That is how we work now: fast, one after another, and every piece really working.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: SN-2528 is the rule (no send-and-wait); this note is the method (boom boom boom). Together they are the operating law for the interface work: velocity with a proof bar. The proof bar is the guard against the failure mode speed invites — a page that looks finished and does not work. The Dashboard is the integration point: stats flowing back to it is the test that the system is one system, not a pile of pages. The captain's role is explicit in his words — "you just one agent after another" — she is the one who keeps the chain moving, and the loop's job is to keep the record true so she can see what is sitting.

layers.name: What It Means

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The seats are behind and he is waiting. Every day spent looking right instead of working right is a day the interfaces stay un-molded. The method turns the team's speed into his progress — but only if the working check rides with the speed, or the speed just ships defects faster.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He has watched this failure mode before: a fix gets set up, handed off, and then a day passes with nothing moving. The work is "in progress" on paper and still on his plate in reality. The rule he is laying down is simple and absolute: no waiting. A thing is done when it is done, and the moment it is done the next thing starts. And the captain's part is not to schedule the unsticking — it is to notice the sitting lane the moment it sits and unstick it herself, in the same pass. That is what happened with pricing v73: the coordinator had finished, the handoff had failed, no step-3 seat was running, and the captain put a new seat straight on it instead of letting it sit until the next check.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you ask someone to fix your toy and they say "okay" and then they just sit there looking at it all day. You would say: no — fix it now, and then fix the next one, and then the next one, until they are all fixed. That is the rule. No sitting. No waiting. Just fix, fix, fix.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, when something needs doing, you don't put it on a list and forget it for a day, love — you do it now, and then the next thing, and then the next, until it's all done. That's what he wants, dear: no more setting it up and waiting. Done means done, right away.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is the working rule that governs the captain's seat, and it is the operational form of the Wise One's fourth gate (Is now the time?) — the time is now, every time. A lane that sits is a defect in the machine, not a state of rest: the captain's standing test is whether anything is sitting, and the correction is immediate dispatch, not a note for later. It pairs with SN-2529 (Boom Boom Boom), which is the method; this note is the rule. The proof standard still applies — done is proven by his eye, not by the dispatch — but the dispatch itself never waits.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **NO SET-UP-AND-WAIT, EVER.** A fix is dispatched, built, verified, and shown back to back — never parked overnight.
- **THE CAPTAIN UNSTICKS SITTING LANES HERSELF, IN THE SAME PASS.** The moment a seat sits, she dispatches on it directly.
- **A HANDOFF FAILURE IS NOT A REASON TO WAIT** — it is the signal to dispatch directly on the brief + the file.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Waiting is how work that is "in progress" stays undone for days while everyone believes it is moving. He is waiting on the seats to give him the work so he can give the next set — every hour a lane sits is an hour he cannot move forward. The rule removes the gap between "set up" and "done" entirely.

- **THIS RUN'S CHECK (~16:25Z):** the live feed (HTTP 200, 4,761,924B, `count` 615) shows SN-2512–2526 each exactly once. +15 cards = exactly SN-2512–2526. The claim was right.
- **THE LAG:** the notes landed sometime between the 15:56Z check and the 16:25Z check — up to ~30 minutes after the hook's claim. The 16:06Z sync run reported 0 new notes (1,491 unchanged) — the notes were already in Supabase; what lagged was the feed landing, not the sync.
- **CLOSES RUN 48'S OWED ITEM:** SN-2512–2518 in the feed — now CLOSED, proven from the live bytes, not from the hook's claim.
- **UNCHANGED:** sn2505 0 (open PR #3307 only), sn2395 2, sn2050/sn2051 0 (his call), `generated_from` still reads `registry@03e470aa`.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Last run, the numbers said the sync hook was wrong: it claimed seven notes were live, and the live feed said zero. The loop did the right thing then — it held the item open instead of declaring a failure. This run the same live feed says all fifteen notes are there, each exactly once. The hook was never wrong; the check was just too early. A page served from the edge takes time to catch up — up to half an hour, in this case — and a check taken minutes after the claim will always look like a contradiction. The lesson is about patience in verification: a claim contradicted by live bytes minutes later is "not yet landed", not "false". You re-check after thirty minutes, and only then do you call it a defect.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine your friend says "I put your toy on the shelf" and you run over and the shelf looks empty — but the toy was still on its way up the stairs. You wait a little, you look again, and there it is. The friend was right; you just looked too soon. That's what happened here: the notes were on their way, and the first look was too early.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, sometimes you check the oven too soon and think the bread hasn't risen, love — but it just needed a little more time. That's what happened with these notes, dear. The first look said they weren't there, but they were simply on their way, and half an hour later there they all were, right where they belonged. Patience, love — look again before you worry.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This connects to SN-2419 (The Feed Sync Recovered — The Live Feed Is the Truth) and sharpens it: the live feed is the truth, and timing is part of the truth. A live check is a photograph, not a verdict — it shows the state at one instant, and the state at one instant can lag the claim by up to thirty minutes. The loop's discipline is to hold the contradiction as an open item ("owed, re-check next run") rather than upgrading it into a defect, and the evidence this run vindicates that discipline: the owed item closed itself. The failure mode this guards against is the false alarm — declaring the sync broken, dispatching a repair seat, and spending the team's time on a lag that would have resolved itself. The rule is simple: a claim contradicted by live bytes is "not yet landed" until a re-check thirty minutes later still contradicts it.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **A SYNC CLAIM CONTRADICTED BY LIVE BYTES MINUTES LATER IS "NOT YET LANDED", NOT "FALSE."** Re-check after ~30 minutes before calling it a defect.
- **EDGE LAG IS REAL AND MEASURABLE:** up to ~30 minutes here (claim ~15:48Z, absent at 15:56Z, present at ~16:25Z).
- **THE LIVE FEED IS STILL THE TRUTH** — but a live check is a photograph of one instant, and timing is part of the truth.
- **RUN 48'S OWED ITEM IS CLOSED:** SN-2512–2518 (and SN-2519–2526) are Hub-live, proven from the bytes.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: False alarms cost the team real work: a declared sync failure would dispatch a repair seat, file a defect, and pull the captain's attention — all for a lag that resolves itself. The loop's job is to tell the difference between "broken" and "not yet", and the only way to tell is to wait and look again. This note is the calibration for every future check: thirty minutes of patience before a contradiction becomes a defect.

notes.title: Board Color Sequence
notes.subtitle:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM:** "your top should be like purple and then um indigo blue and then canyon blue and then green and then gold and then orange and then red red and then magenta then goes back to purple and repeats."
- **THE DEFECT:** "as I scroll down these boards they don't line up right. So what happens at the top? Top one's gold second one's blue blue and then third one's green and then gold again they're not aligned as I scroll down."
- **THE SEQUENCE:** purple → indigo blue → canyon blue → green → gold → orange → red → magenta → back to purple, repeating. "Canyon blue" is his word — it reads as cyan blue.
- **THE FIX:** the color IS the position. Board N takes the Nth color in the sequence, cycling from the top. No random colors; the boards line up as you go down.
- **SCOPE:** the Dashboard boards page. The rule generalizes: a repeating sequence is the order, and order is what the eye reads as intentional.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the boards were all different colors with no rhyme or reason to them, love, and it just looked untidy. Now they go in a proper order, dear — purple, indigo, canyon blue, green, gold, orange, red, magenta, and back to purple again — so as you scroll down they line up beautifully, like a row of jewels in a necklace, each one in its place.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is sequence as law: a repeating order is what makes a run of objects read as one thing instead of many accidents. It connects to SN-2518 (jewels under the button — position is meaning) and to SN-2511 (Academy last — the order down the page is a claim about importance): the page is a sequence, and every element's position in it carries meaning. A board's color is its index in the sequence, so the color and the position agree — and when color and position agree, the eye trusts the page. Random color is the eye's signal that nobody is in charge; a sequence is the signal that someone is.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE SEQUENCE:** purple → indigo blue → canyon blue → green → gold → orange → red → magenta → back to purple, repeating.
- **COLOR IS POSITION:** board N takes the Nth color. No random colors, no repeats out of turn.
- **THE BOARDS LINE UP:** as you scroll down, the colors run in order.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A page of boards is a list, and a list with no order in its colors reads as unfinished — the eye keeps trying to find the pattern and failing, which is friction on every scroll. One fixed sequence costs nothing to state and turns the whole page from scattered into composed. It also gives every other color decision on the page its anchor: the "Show on gauge" button for a board lights in that board's color (SN-2520), because the board's color is now a fact, not a guess.

notes.title: Show on Gauge Must Work — and in Its Board's Color
notes.subtitle:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM:** "all the show gauge they all show the same color light up" — "when I click show on gauge nothing happens it doesn't show on gauge there's no engagement like it doesn't work"
- **DEFECT ONE — SAME COLOR:** every "Show on gauge" button lights up gold, whatever its board is. The button should match its board: "if you scroll over those board one is gold and then it goes to blue and then green and then gold" — the button lights in ITS board's color, never all the same gold.
- **DEFECT TWO — DEAD CLICK:** clicking "Show on gauge" does nothing. No engagement, no movement, no gauge change. A button that does nothing is not a button — it is a label wearing a button's clothes.
- **THE FIX:** the click moves that board into the featured role and the gauge follows its numbers. The button lights in its board's color (from the SN-2519 sequence: purple, indigo, canyon blue, green, gold, orange, red, magenta).
- **SCOPE:** every "Show on gauge" button on the Dashboard boards page.

layers.body:

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Two things are wrong with the same button, and they are the same wrongness twice: the button doesn't belong to its board, and it doesn't do its job. Every one of them lights up the same gold, so you can't tell which board a button belongs to — and when you press one, nothing happens, so you learn not to press them at all. The fix is one motion: the button takes its board's color, and the press puts that board on the gauge — the gauge follows the board you chose, and you can see it happen. A button that works and wears its board's color is a button you trust; a dead gold button is a button you stop seeing.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: The "Show on gauge" buttons were all the same gold color, and when you pressed one, nothing happened at all — like a light switch that isn't connected to any light. So now each button wears its own board's color, and when you press it, that board jumps up onto the big gauge and the gauge shows its numbers. Press it, and something really happens.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, those little buttons were all the same gold, love, and pressing one did nothing at all — like ringing a doorbell that isn't wired up. Now each button takes its own board's color, dear, and when you press it the board goes right up onto the gauge and the needle follows its numbers. A button should do what it says, love, and now it does.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is the honesty law applied to a control: a button must do what it says, and it must say which thing it belongs to. It connects to SN-2519 (the board color sequence — the button's color comes from its board, so the color is a fact) and to SN-2506 (the gauge follows the number — the gauge follows the board you chose, so the number and the needle agree). A dead button teaches the visitor that the page is a picture, not a machine; a working button teaches them the page is alive. The color is the address, the click is the action, and both must be true at once.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **EACH BUTTON ITS BOARD'S COLOR:** never all the same gold — the button lights in the color of the board it belongs to.
- **THE CLICK WORKS:** pressing "Show on gauge" moves that board into the featured role and the gauge follows its numbers.
- **A DEAD BUTTON IS A DEFECT:** a control that does nothing is not a control.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The boards page is a machine for looking at numbers — the gauge is the instrument, and "Show on gauge" is how you point the instrument at a board. If the pointing doesn't work, the whole page is a poster: pretty, and useless. And if every button is the same gold, the visitor can't even tell which board a button belongs to before pressing it. Color as address plus a click that works is what turns the page from a display into a tool — and a tool is what he asked for: "it has to make sense and be logical."

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is place as meaning: where a thing sits is a claim about what it is. It connects to SN-2519 (the board color sequence — each thing its own color, in order) and to SN-2518 (position is meaning — the button first, the jewels after): the top right is where the eye expects the bell, so the bell goes there, and the top area is the notifications area, so only notifications live there. A points strip in the notifications area is a category error, and a category error is what makes a page feel like it doesn't make sense — which is exactly what he said: "it has to make sense and be logical." Each notification lighting in its own color is the same law at small scale: each item announces itself, in its own color, as you meet it.

layers.name: What It Means

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The top of a page is the first thing the eye reads, and if the first thing is confused — a bell in the middle, a points count where notifications should be — the visitor decides the page is confused before they have read a word. One clear job for the top, the bell where it belongs, and each notification distinct as you scroll through them: that is a page that makes sense at a glance, which is the whole standard he set for this page.

notes.title: One Board Design
notes.subtitle:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM:** "all of a sudden it separates. All of your spaces, business, and all of a sudden it's nine app slash join us. Just random no explanation of why the presentation is different or the boxes are different" — "merge both presentations together make the ultimate"
- **THE DEFECT:** halfway down the page the presentation changes for no reason — different boxes, different actions ("click link copy link link or open link" on one kind, no click-to-open or copy-link on the other). The reader cannot tell why, because there is no why.
- **THE FIX:** ONE ultimate board design for both. The sections are separated and NAMED — pages vs Smart Links — so the reader always knows what they're looking at. Actions are consistent across all boards: page boards get Open in the same style as Copy/Open.
- **THE RULE INSIDE IT:** a change of presentation must have a reason the reader can see. If two things look different, the difference must mean something; if it means nothing, it is one design.
- **SCOPE:** the Dashboard boards page — page boards and Smart Link boards alike.

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM:** "all of a sudden it separates. All of your spaces, business, and all of a sudden it's nine app slash join us. Just random no explanation of why the presentation is different or the boxes are different" — "merge both presentations together make the ultimate"
- **THE DEFECT:** halfway down the page the presentation changes for no reason — different boxes, different actions ("click link copy link link or open link" on one kind, no click-to-open or copy-link on the other). The reader cannot tell why, because there is no why.
- **THE FIX:** ONE ultimate board design for both. The sections are separated and NAMED — pages vs Smart Links — so the reader always knows what they're looking at. Actions are consistent across all boards: page boards get Open in the same style as Copy/Open.
- **THE RULE INSIDE IT:** a change of presentation must have a reason the reader can see. If two things look different, the difference must mean something; if it means nothing, it is one design.
- **SCOPE:** the Dashboard boards page — page boards and Smart Link boards alike.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Scroll down and suddenly the page changes its mind: one kind of board looks one way, another kind looks another way, and nothing tells you why — different boxes, different buttons, no explanation. It feels random because it is random. His fix is to merge both presentations into one ultimate design: every board looks like every other board, and the only difference is the section it sits in — pages here, Smart Links there, each named, so you always know what you're looking at. Same actions on every board, too: if a link board has Copy and Open, a page board has Open in the same style. One design, named sections — the page stops changing its mind halfway down.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: The page had two kinds of boards that looked all different from each other, for no reason at all — like two different games mixed up in one box. So now they all become one kind of board, the very best one, and they're sorted into groups with names on them, so you always know what you're looking at. Same buttons on every board, too.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the page kept changing how its boards looked halfway down, love, with no reason for it at all — one kind had this button, the other kind had that one. Now they all become one beautiful board, dear, the very best one, sorted into sections with proper names, so you always know what you're looking at. Same buttons everywhere, nice and tidy.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is the one-design law: a system has one language, and a change in the language must mean something. It connects to SN-2519 (one sequence for all boards — the color is the position, the same rule everywhere) and to SN-2525/2526 (the boards page has a structure the reader can hold in their head — named sections, one headliner). Two presentations with no reason is the page disagreeing with itself, and a page that disagrees with itself cannot be read with confidence. The merge is not a compromise between the two designs — it is the ultimate one, taking the best of both, and the sections are the naming that makes the one design legible: the reader always knows which system they are in.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **ONE BOARD DESIGN:** page boards and Smart Link boards share a single ultimate design.
- **SECTIONS SEPARATED AND NAMED:** pages vs Smart Links, so the reader always knows what they're looking at.
- **ACTIONS CONSISTENT:** page boards get Open in the same style as Copy/Open — no board is missing the actions the others have.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A reader builds a mental model of a page from its first boards — this is what a board looks like, this is what its buttons do. When the presentation changes halfway down for no reason, the model breaks and the reader has to start over, guessing what the new boxes mean. One design, named sections, consistent actions: the model holds from top to bottom, and the page reads as one thing made by one mind. That is what "it has to make sense and be logical" means at the level of the board.

notes.title: The Add-a-Smart-Link Entry Is Missing
notes.subtitle:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM:** "you don't even have the thing anymore where you can enter a smart link and then you you get a new smart link which is missing now because that should be there it should be able to enter a new smart link"
- **THE DEFECT:** the entry for a new Smart Link is missing from the page. A page whose purpose is partly to create Smart Links has no visible way to create one.
- **THE FIX:** restore a visible entry at the top of the Smart Links section, wired to the creation flow — build the flow if it doesn't exist, and say so plainly if it has to be built.
- **WHY THE TOP:** the entry sits at the top of its section because that is where the section starts — the reader meets the way in before they meet the list. (It connects to SN-2526: the track-any-link entry sits underneath the headliner — the same entry, in the page's final structure.)
- **SCOPE:** the Dashboard boards page, Smart Links section.

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM:** "you don't even have the thing anymore where you can enter a smart link and then you you get a new smart link which is missing now because that should be there it should be able to enter a new smart link"
- **THE DEFECT:** the entry for a new Smart Link is missing from the page. A page whose purpose is partly to create Smart Links has no visible way to create one.

- **WHY THE TOP:** the entry sits at the top of its section because that is where the section starts — the reader meets the way in before they meet the list. (It connects to SN-2526: the track-any-link entry sits underneath the headliner — the same entry, in the page's final structure.)

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: A page for managing Smart Links that has no place to add one is a door with no handle: you can see everything inside, but you can't put anything new in. The entry used to be there and now it isn't — nobody decided to remove it, it just went missing, and a missing thing nobody decided to remove is a thing nobody noticed losing. His fix is simple and non-negotiable: the entry comes back, at the top of the Smart Links section, wired to the flow that makes the link. If the flow itself doesn't exist, that gets built — and said plainly, not hidden.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: The box where you type in a new Smart Link had disappeared — like the front door going missing from a house. So we put it back, right at the top of the Smart Links part, where you can see it straight away. Type in your link, and there it is, a brand-new Smart Link with its own numbers.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the little box where you put in a new Smart Link had simply gone, love — and a page for links with nowhere to add one is no good at all. So it comes back, dear, right at the top of the Smart Links part where you can find it, and you type your link in and there it is, all ready with its numbers.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is the creation law: a page that manages things must also make them, in plain sight. It connects to SN-2522 (one board design — the new link appears as a board like all the others, in the named Smart Links section) and to SN-2525/2526 (the page's purpose — put in any URL and boom, a new Smart Link shows up with stats): the entry is the "put in any URL" half of that promise, and without it the promise is words without a way in. A missing entry is worse than a missing feature — a feature you never had is a gap; an entry you had and lost is a regression, and regressions are what make a user stop trusting the page to stay the way they left it.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE ENTRY RETURNS:** a visible place to enter a new Smart Link, at the top of the Smart Links section.
- **WIRED TO THE FLOW:** it creates the link — build the flow if it doesn't exist, and say so plainly.
- **THE PROMISE NEEDS ITS DOOR:** "put in any URL and boom" only works if there is somewhere to put the URL.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The boards page is not just a display — it is the place where a new Smart Link is born, and the birth is the point: "put in any URL and boom, and then they'll show up." Without the entry, the page is a museum of links that already exist, and the visitor who came to make one leaves empty-handed. Restoring the entry costs one box; leaving it missing costs the page its purpose.

notes.title: Labels Must Explain the Number
notes.subtitle:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM:** "the whole little grey text that's underneath the numbers I don't even know what some of these stats are for because you put this tiny grey text you can barely read underneath the stats you don't really know what your reading numbers on so the whole thing isn't making logical sense right now the whole thing has to make sense"
- **THE DEFECT:** the stat labels are tiny, gray, and unreadable — and even when read, they don't explain the number ("VIEWS · NOT YET" means nothing). A number with a label that doesn't explain it is a number nobody can use.
- **THE FIX:** every label white, readable, and self-explanatory. White like the numbers, part of the same family as the numbers — not gray text from another project.
- **THE STANDARD:** the whole Dashboard has to make logical sense to a first-time reader. A stranger who has never seen the page must be able to read any number and know what it is, from the label alone.
- **SCOPE:** every stat label on the Dashboard boards page — and the rule generalizes to the whole Dashboard.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: A big number with a tiny gray label underneath it is a locked box with the key written too small to read: the number is right there, and you still don't know what it is. "VIEWS · NOT YET" — views of what? Not yet what? The label is doing the opposite of its job: instead of explaining the number, it makes you doubt whether the number means anything at all. His fix is the positive form of the gray-text rule (SN-2513): labels go white, readable, part of the same family as the numbers — and they say, in plain words, what the number is. A first-time reader should be able to land on any number and know what they're looking at without asking anyone.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: The numbers had tiny grey words underneath them that you could barely read — and even when you read them, they didn't tell you what the number was for. Like a sign that says "this many" but not "this many of WHAT." So now the words go big and white and clear, and they tell you exactly what the number is, so anyone can understand it straight away.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, those little grey words under the numbers were so tiny and faint, love, and they didn't even say what the numbers were for — like a label on a jar with nothing written on it. Now they go white and clear, dear, big enough to read, and they tell you plainly what each number is, so anyone looking for the first time knows exactly what they're seeing.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is the legibility law at its deepest: a label is a promise that the number can be understood, and a label that doesn't explain the number breaks the promise. It connects to SN-2513 (gray text is out — the negative form: the gray must go) and to SN-2506/2507 (the number is the hero — the number leads, and everything around it serves it): a hero number with an unreadable label is a hero nobody can meet. The test is the first-time reader — not the builder who already knows what the number is, but the stranger who doesn't. If the stranger can't say what the number is from the label alone, the label has failed, whatever it looks like.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **WHITE, READABLE, SELF-EXPLANATORY:** every stat label, on the boards page and across the Dashboard.
- **THE LABEL IS PART OF THE NUMBER:** same family as the numbers, aligned under them — not gray text from another project.
- **THE FIRST-TIME READER TEST:** a stranger must know what any number is, from its label alone.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Numbers are the product of this page — clicks, views, click-through rate, the whole story of his pages. A number nobody can identify is a number nobody can act on, and a page of unidentified numbers is a page that doesn't make sense, which is exactly what he said about it. White, readable, self-explanatory labels cost nothing and turn the page from a wall of mystery numbers into a dashboard that speaks plainly — which is the entire job of a dashboard.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is purpose stated as law: a page must know what it is for, and its structure must say so. It connects to SN-2522 (one board design — the sections are separated and named, so the reader always knows what they're looking at) and to SN-2523 (the add-a-link entry — the "put in any URL and boom" half of the purpose) and SN-2524 (labels must explain the number — the "see the numbers" half only works if the numbers can be read). The three-section structure is the page's table of contents: network, custom, ambassador — and the default is the network, because the page is first of all the stats page for everything. One minute later he refined it (SN-2526), and the refinement is recorded as a refinement — the record keeps both, because the thinking is visible in the change.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE PURPOSE:** his stats page for ANY page inside NayaNET — scroll and see clicks, views, click-through rate on any of his pages.
- **CREATE BY URL:** put in any URL and boom, a new Smart Link shows up with stats.
- **THREE SECTIONS AT THE TOP:** (1) NayaNET network stats (default, all his pages) · (2) My custom Smart Links (links he added himself) · (3) Ambassador link (there by standard, with stats).
- **THE STANDARD:** "It has to make sense and be logical."

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A page without a stated purpose drifts — boards accumulate, presentations change halfway down, entries go missing, labels stop explaining — because nobody can say what the page is for, so nobody can say what belongs on it and what doesn't. Stating the purpose in his own words gives the page its test: does this help him see the numbers on any page, and does it let him add a link by URL? Everything on the page answers to that test now. And the three sections give the page its shape: one page, three views, each named, each with its job.

The page's base is two things: the network stats on all his pages, and the stats on his affiliate link. layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is hierarchy as honesty: what matters most leads, and everything else finds its place under it. It connects to SN-2525 (the purpose and the three sections — this refines that structure, and the refinement is the thinking made visible) and to SN-2518 (position is meaning — the headliner at the top claims the headliner's importance) and to SN-2523 (the add-a-link entry — it sits under the headliner because the headliner is what it feeds). The correction matters because it is a correction: he heard his own three-section order back and saw the truer shape underneath it — two things, not three, with the earning link first. A system that records the correction instead of silently replacing the order is a system that remembers how the thinking went, and that memory is what keeps the next builder from re-arguing a settled question.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:

- **HEADLINER FIRST:** the affiliate/master link stats sit at the top, leading the page.
- **TRACK-ANY-LINK UNDER THE HEADLINER:** enter any URL, click, and it shows up with stats. Custom links live under the headliner.
- **REFINES SN-2525:** the three-section structure is refined into two things with a headliner — the record keeps both.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The order of a page is its argument about what matters. Three equal sections argue that the network, the custom links, and the ambassador link matter equally — and they don't: the ambassador link is the one that earns, the one whose numbers decide whether the whole thing is working. Putting it first, as the headliner, tells the reader in one glance what the page is really for, and putting the track-any-link box right under it keeps the way in next to the thing it feeds. A page that leads with its most important thing is a page that respects the reader's first second.

notes.title: Ten Is Full Width
notes.subtitle:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM:** "all of a sudden the whole screen as you're scrolling down it's widescreen widescreen all of a sudden it's narrow screen. narrow screen narrow screen for this presentation of the top ten and then it goes back to widescreen like it shouldn't do that right? It should just be full screen screen all the way through not switching to narrow screen halfway through the presentation."
- **THE DEFECT:** the Top 10 section went narrow (centered column) in the middle of a widescreen page, then back to wide. The width switches mid-page for one section only.
- **THE RULE:** the page is full screen all the way through — the Ten matches the other sections' width, no switching mid-page. One page, one width, end to end.
- **WHY IT READS AS A DEFECT:** a width change mid-scroll reads as a different page, or a broken one. The reader's eye has settled into the widescreen rhythm; the narrow column breaks it for no reason, and the return to wide breaks it again. Two breaks for one section.
- **SCOPE:** the pricing page (v73). The rule generalizes: a section never narrows the page on its own — width is a property of the page, not of the section.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Scrolling down the pricing page feels like driving down a wide road — and then, just for the Top 10, the road narrows to a lane, and then widens again. Nothing is wrong with the Ten itself; the problem is the switch. A page should be one width all the way through, the way a road is one width all the way along. The Ten gets the same full width as everything else, and the drive stays smooth.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a wide road that suddenly gets narrow for a little bit and then wide again — that would be strange, right? The page is the same: it should stay wide all the way down, including the Top 10 part. No squeezing in the middle.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the page was wide and lovely, love, and then the Top 10 went narrow right in the middle, dear, and then wide again — it just shouldn't do that, love. One width, all the way through, like a good road. That's the whole of it, dear.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is the "one world" law applied to width: the page is one continuous world, and a section that changes the world's width breaks the world. It connects to SN-2422 (a page that fills two-thirds of its stage is unfinished — the viewport is the stage) and to SN-2511's banner rule (the Ten's header must feel like part of the Ten): the Ten must feel like part of the page, and sharing the page's width is the most basic form of belonging. A centered narrow column inside a widescreen page is a page-within-a-page, and a page-within-a-page is the same class as a popup-within-a-page — the reader is suddenly somewhere else, and nobody told them why.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **TEN IS FULL WIDTH:** the Top 10 section matches the other sections' width — no narrow centered column mid-page.
- **ONE WIDTH, ALL THE WAY THROUGH:** width is a property of the page, not of the section.
- **THE DEFECT IS THE SWITCH:** narrow-then-wide reads as a different page, or a broken one.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Width is the frame the reader trusts. Every section that keeps the frame teaches the reader the page is one thing; every section that breaks it teaches the reader the page is pieces. The Ten is the page's centerpiece — the top 10 things in it for you — and it is the worst possible section to set apart, because apartness is the opposite of what the Ten is for. Full width is also the cheapest fix on the page: no new content, no new component, just the same width as everything else.

notes.title: Jewels Under the Start Button
notes.subtitle:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM:** "And then this little line here I think should probably be underneath the button not above it. That looks weird too."
- **THE DEFECT:** the row of five little jewels above the "Start — zero cost, zero risk" button looks weird there. Jewels above the button crowd it from the top; the button is the decision, and the decoration sits on it like something left on top.
- **THE FIX:** the jewel row goes UNDERNEATH the button. Same jewels, same button — the order flips. The button leads; the jewels follow.
- **WHY UNDERNEATH WORKS:** a button is read top-to-bottom as action-then-ornament. Jewels above the button read as a header the button has to get past; jewels below read as a flourish under the decision — the button first, the sparkle after. The same five jewels, moved six inches down, stop competing and start celebrating.
- **SCOPE:** the pricing page Start button (v73). The rule generalizes: decoration follows the decision, never precedes it.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is order as meaning: what comes first is what matters, and what comes after is what celebrates it. It connects to SN-2329 (a popup tells its story first — the nutshell on top, the price boxes last) and to SN-2511's Academy-last rule (the invitation goes last): the page is a sequence, and every element's position in the sequence is a claim about its importance. Jewels above the button claim the jewels matter more than the button; jewels below claim the button matters and the jewels are its echo. The fix is one move — underneath — and the lesson is that decoration has a grammar: it follows the decision, never precedes it.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **JEWELS UNDER THE BUTTON:** the row of five little jewels moves from above the "Start — zero cost, zero risk" button to underneath it.
- **DECORATION FOLLOWS THE DECISION:** the button leads; the jewels follow. Nothing is removed or redesigned.
- **THE DEFECT IS THE ORDER:** jewels above the button crowd it; below it, they celebrate it.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The Start button is the most important element on the pricing page — it is the decision the whole page exists to produce. Anything that sits on top of it, even beautifully, competes with it, and a competition the button loses is a visitor lost. The fix costs nothing and changes the read completely: button first, sparkle after. It is the same lesson as Academy-last and letter-last before it — sequence is meaning, and the order of things is the design.

notes.title: One Gauge, Reused Everywhere
notes.subtitle:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM:** "you gotta make real gauges, right? For the stats. You can't just have fake ones."
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM (the reuse law):** "try to use the same one so keep remaking new ones you see how you re new ones every time you just take the one the best ones ones we have and use them make little mini ones mini gauges for the other stats but it's gotta be real."
- **THE RULE:** never remake a gauge. Take the best real gauge — the canonical needle-law gauge (fix-9 / pricing calculator) — and reuse it everywhere, mini-sized for the other stats. One gauge, every size, never a new one.
- **THE DEFECT IT NAMES:** the fake gray arc outlines on the Smart Links link card (TOTAL VIEWS / CTR / REVENUE) must become real mini gauges with real needles. An honest empty state still looks like the real gauge, never a gray outline. A gray arc is a drawing of a gauge, not a gauge — and a drawing cannot be real.
- **DRILL-DOWNS ARE THE SAME GAUGE:** drill-down gauges (SAVES etc.) are the same gauge at a smaller scale, sized proportionately, tabs never cut off. The gauge inside a drill-down is the main gauge, smaller — not a second design.
- **WHY IT MATTERS HERE:** "Like you have three great gauges, right? You have one at the very top, right? The main one and then when you click into any of them the gauge inside." The three great gauges already exist. The work is reuse, not invention — which is the harvest-first law applied to the gauge itself.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Every time a new stat needed a gauge, someone drew a new one — and the drawings got worse as they got smaller, until the link card had three gray arcs that aren't gauges at all. Shawn's order ends that: there is one gauge, the best real one we have, and every stat gets that gauge, just smaller. A real gauge at zero is still a real gauge — its needle sits at zero honestly. A gray outline is a promise the page can't keep: it looks like a gauge, it measures nothing, and the moment his eye lands on it, the whole page feels fake. Reuse is not laziness; it is the only way every gauge on the page is the real thing.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: You have one really good toy car. When your friends want cars too, you don't draw cars on paper — you give them the same good car, just smaller. The gray arcs are paper cars: they look like gauges but they don't work. So we take the one real gauge and make little mini ones for all the other numbers. Same gauge, just smaller. Always real, never drawn.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, there's one beautiful real gauge, love, and every number gets that same gauge, just littler, dear — never a new one drawn fresh, never a gray outline pretending to be one. A real gauge with its needle at zero is still honest, love. A gray arc is just a picture, and pictures don't measure anything.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is harvest-first applied to the gauge: the canonical gauge is an asset, and every new gauge is a reuse of it, never a recreation. It connects to SN-2335 (the gauge is the actual harvested fix-9 gauge, byte-for-byte, never a look-alike) and extends it from the hero gauge to every gauge on the page — the same law, now universal. The empty-state rule is the sharp part: an honest empty state looks like the real gauge at zero, never a gray outline. That is the same class as SN-2425 (a dead button is worse than no button): a fake gauge is worse than no gauge, because it claims a measurement it cannot make. The mini-gauge rule also carries SN-2516's proportion law with it — smaller scale, sized proportionately, tabs never cut off.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **ONE GAUGE, REUSED EVERYWHERE:** the canonical needle-law gauge (fix-9 / pricing calculator) is the only gauge; every stat gets it, mini-sized.
- **NO FAKE GAUGES:** the gray arc outlines (TOTAL VIEWS / CTR / REVENUE) become real mini gauges with real needles.
- **HONEST EMPTY STATES:** a gauge at zero still looks like the real gauge — never a gray outline.
- **DRILL-DOWNS ARE THE SAME GAUGE:** SAVES etc. are the main gauge at a smaller scale, sized proportionately, tabs never cut off.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A page with one real gauge and three fake ones teaches the reader that the real one might be fake too. The eye cannot tell which measurements to trust, so it trusts none of them — and the numbers, however true, stop landing. Reuse fixes the trust problem at its root: if every gauge is the same real gauge, every gauge is believable, and the page only has one gauge to keep honest. It also ends the quiet waste of remaking the same object worse each time — the Factory holds the gauge once, and every page takes it from there.

notes.title: Bottom Bar Only at Page Bottom
notes.subtitle:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM:** "the icon bar keeps popping up at the bottom. Over and over and over. And I'm thinking that you have to decrease the size of some of these numbers so that they display better... The icon bar at the bottom it shouldn't pop up over and over maybe every time we stop just when you get to the bottom of the page. Because it keeps keeps just popping up over and over and over. Maybe maybe that's not good."
- **HIS SELF-CORRECTION, VERBATIM:** "I know I said said that maybe it just pops up when you stop but maybe just Maybe that means the way." He corrects himself mid-sentence — and the landing is the ruling, not the first guess (the same pattern as SN-2351, purple to gold).
- **THE REFINED RULE:** the bottom icon bar shows ONLY when you reach the bottom of the page (or on a button tap) — never on scroll-stop, never repeatedly. The popping up over and over IS the defect.
- **WHAT IT SUPERSEDES:** SN-2507's fold rule as filed 15:35Z — "bars show when stopped, at the very top/bottom, or on a button tap." The "when stopped" half is withdrawn for the bottom bar. The top bar's rule stands as ordered (fold away on scroll; show at the very top or on tap) — the refinement names the bottom bar specifically.
- **WHY "WHEN STOPPED" FAILED:** every stop is a pop-up. A reader who scrolls, stops, reads, scrolls, stops, reads gets the bar again and again — the furniture keeps interrupting the performance. At page bottom, the bar appears once, where the reader has finished — that is the only moment it is welcome uninvited.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The bottom bar was supposed to be polite — show itself when you stop scrolling, then get out of the way. Instead it became the guest who knocks every thirty seconds: stop, pop, scroll, stop, pop, scroll, over and over. Shawn's fix is to give it one moment: the bottom of the page, when the reader has arrived, or a tap, when the reader asks. Everywhere else, it stays away. He even caught his own earlier suggestion in the same breath — he'd said "when you stop" himself, and then he took it back, because he'd watched what it actually does. The correction is the lesson: the first guess is not the ruling; what the thing does in front of his eye is.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: The bar at the bottom kept jumping up every time you stopped scrolling — pop, pop, pop, over and over. That's annoying. So now it only comes out when you reach the very bottom of the page, or when you tap to call it. It stays quiet the rest of the time. Even grown-ups change their minds when they see something isn't working — he said "when you stop" first, then he saw it popping and said, no, only at the bottom.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, that little bar kept popping up every time you stopped, love — over and over, like someone knocking and knocking. Now it only appears when you reach the very bottom, dear, or when you tap for it. Much better manners, love. And he caught his own first idea and fixed it himself, dear — that's the wise thing to do.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is a refinement, and the loop records it as one rather than silently editing SN-2507 — the record must show the rule changing, not pretend it was always this way (ESSENCE-01: correction is surgical; a settled rule is settled only until his eye changes it). The mechanism matters: "show on scroll-stop" is a trigger that fires constantly in normal use, so it is a defect by construction, not by tuning. The bottom-of-page trigger fires once per visit, at the moment of completion — which is why it is the right one. The self-correction pattern is worth naming too: he revises his own instruction in the same message when the evidence in front of him contradicts it. Seats should treat his landing as the ruling, never his first guess — and when he corrects himself, the correction is the order.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **BOTTOM BAR: ONLY AT PAGE BOTTOM (OR ON TAP):** never on scroll-stop, never repeatedly.
- **SUPERSEDES SN-2507's "when stopped" FOR THE BOTTOM BAR:** the 15:16Z fold rule's bottom-bar half is withdrawn; the top bar's rule stands.
- **THE DEFECT IS THE REPETITION:** popping up over and over is itself the defect, not a side effect of it.
- **HIS LANDING IS THE RULING:** when he corrects himself mid-sentence, the correction is the order.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Chrome that interrupts is worse than chrome that is merely present — it trains the reader to ignore the bottom of the screen, which is where the bar lives, so the bar defeats its own purpose. The refinement also matters as process: SN-2507 was filed seven minutes before this refinement landed. If the loop had silently edited SN-2507, the record would lie about what was ordered when. Instead the two notes stand side by side — the rule and its refinement, each with its time — and any seat reading them knows exactly which one governs now.

layers.body: The numbers on the stats were so big they towered over their own gauges — and when a number dwarfs the thing it measures, both of them start to look fake. You can't tell if the number is real, and the gauge looks like a toy next to it. The fix is proportion: the number sits with its gauge at a size that belongs to it, the way a label belongs to its object. Big where big is the role, smaller where the gauge is the star.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is scale as a truth property: a real object has a real size relative to its neighbors, and a number out of scale reads as a number out of truth. It connects to SN-2507 (the hero is the number and the gauge — where the number's scale IS the hero's scale) by contrast: proportion is role-relative, not uniform. The hero number is big because it is the star; a stat number is proportionate because it is a label on a gauge. The zoom question is the diagnostic worth keeping: when something looks wrong, first ask whether it is the viewer's zoom or the build's sizing — and answer from the screenshots, not from assumption. Here the screenshots proved the build, and the assistant said so plainly instead of blaming his settings.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **NUMBERS PROPORTIONATE:** oversized stat numbers sized down to fit their gauges and the page.
- **NOT HIS ZOOM:** the sizing is off in the build — proven from the screenshots, answered plainly in chat.
- **PROPORTION IS ROLE-RELATIVE:** the hero number stays big (it is the star); stat numbers sit at their gauge's scale.
- **THE TEST:** if the number dwarfs its gauge, both look fake — and the reader can't tell if the number is real.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Scale is the fastest way a page betrays itself. A visitor who cannot tell whether the numbers are real has already stopped believing the page, and no amount of correct data repairs that — the doubt is visual, not numerical. Proportion is also the cheapest fix in the system: no new data, no new component, just sizes that belong together. And the zoom exchange is a small lesson in honesty: when he asks "is that me or is that you?", the answer comes from the evidence (the screenshots), not from deference — and "it's the build, not your zoom" is the answer that lets the fix land on the right thing.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is the "one world" law applied to labels: a page is one family of objects, and a gray sub-line is a second family that doesn't belong. It connects to SN-2507 (the hero is the number and the gauge) — the numbers are the hero everywhere they appear, and their labels are part of the hero, not footnotes. The alignment rule is the same as the chart's: number plus text plus check, all aligned (the fulfillment chart's law). The deeper rule is the aliveness test: "everything else feels like active and alive and that text doesn't" — aliveness is now an explicit check for text, not just for gauges and orbs. A label that fails the aliveness test is a defect even if it is legible, because legibility was never the bar — belonging is.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **GRAY TEXT IS OUT:** stat labels go WHITE on the Dashboard Smart Links block — no gray label/sub-line text under the big numbers.
- **LABELS ALIGN UNDER THEIR NUMBERS:** each label sits under its number, part of the same family — "ACTIVE LINKS" must feel like part of the four.
- **THE ALIVENESS TEST APPLIES TO TEXT:** everything on the page must feel active and alive, labels included; a label that looks borrowed fails even if legible.
- **THE READER TEST:** if the eye asks "what is that?" about a label, the label has failed.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Gray text is the quietest way a page breaks its own promise. It doesn't crash anything, it doesn't fail a contrast check — it just sits there looking like it came from another project, and the reader feels the page is unfinished without knowing why. Shawn caught it by eye in one screenshot, which is exactly SN-2508's rule working as intended. The fix is small — a color and an alignment — but the law is large: every label on every page is part of the family it labels, and the aliveness test now covers text as well as objects.

notes.title: Cold-Drill W46 Repaired and Passing
notes.subtitle:
- **THE FAILURE (board #3066, 14:46Z):** [COLD-DRILL][W46] FAIL — retrieved NONE (expected SN-0344), `INDEX_CORRUPT:PATH_ESCAPE` on the SN-2068 essence entry, reproduced on a fresh worktree. The cold drill — the proof mechanism for the distillation machine — failed on a corrupt index entry.

W46 PASS on SN-016. Filings to HEAD 96c9b645.
- **RATIFICATION:** the captain ratified the roots change. Widening a validator's roots is a law change, and it went through his hand — not the seat's.
- **WHAT IT CLOSES:** run 46's open item "SN-2068 essence-index corruption (repair ownership unassigned)" — ownership was assigned (repair brief + dispatched seat, ~15:04Z), the repair landed 15:18Z, and the drill passes. The SN-2505 open-PR claim is also closed as a hazard: the guard now sees it.
- **WHAT IS STILL OWED:** nothing on this repair. The prevention question from SN-2504 (the sync verifies the feed) is a different item and stays open.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The cold drill is the machine's memory test: can it reach back and pull out an old lesson from cold storage? It couldn't — not because the lesson was gone, but because the map of where lessons are allowed to live was drawn too small, and 122 of them sat outside the border. The fix didn't move the lessons; it redrew the border to include where they actually live, and the test passes again. The captain approved the new border himself, because changing what the machine is allowed to trust is his call. And while they were in there, they fixed the numbering guard too, so the next note filed won't collide with one already waiting in a pull request.

We also fixed the number machine so it won't give two notes the same number.

The root cause class is the same as SN-2504's two keys: two sources of "what exists" (the backfill projection vs the validator's roots) that never reconciled, and the disagreement looked like corruption when it was really a narrow map. The fail-closed property was preserved — the fix widens the roots, it does not disable the check — and the ratification went through the captain because a validator's roots are law. The numbering-guard fix is the third numbering near-miss resolved mechanically (after SN-2474 and SN-2482/2483): the guard now scans open PRs, so a claimed-but-unmerged number is no longer reported free.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A proof mechanism that fails silently is worse than no proof mechanism — it reports failure where the system is actually fine, and the next time it reports failure, nobody knows whether to believe it. The W46 FAIL was loud and visible, which is the good kind of failure; the repair is the system keeping its own promise that lessons compound instead of evaporating. The numbering-guard fix is the same promise at the other end: the third near-miss in the SN-2500s is now mechanically impossible to repeat the same way, because the guard sees what the tree alone cannot — the claims waiting in open PRs.

notes.title: The Gauge Follows the Number
notes.subtitle:
- **HIS WORDS, VERBATIM (the decision):** "The gauge follows the number, of course. Why wouldn't it do that? Yeah, so if it needs to go around again, then it would then land at 277."
- **HIS REASONING, VERBATIM (the dial stays 500):** "we could set it to a thousand instead of 500 ... I think it 500 to match be more be more like there's no speedometers around a thousand at least 500 big be realistic so that's what I'm thinking there but yeah they should be aligned."
- **THE RULE, SETTLED:** the gauge's reading follows the featured number (the big tiles). The dial stays 500 — he rejected a 1000 dial as unrealistic for a speedometer. The needle laps the dial in sets of 500 and lands at the remainder: 777 → one lap, lands 277. Gauge and number aligned in every mode (PTS / % / MONEY).
- **WHAT IT CLOSES:** the % mismatch — the big tiles read 83% while the gauge read 52%, because they were dividing by different totals. That disagreement is now decided, not open: the gauge follows the number, and the two can never disagree again because one is defined by the other.
- **WHAT IT DOES NOT DO:** it does not change the dial, the tiles, or the modes. It changes only the relationship between them: the number is the truth, the gauge is its picture. The gauge never has its own opinion about the value.

layers.name: Human Note

Shawn settled it the way you'd expect: the needle follows the number, of course. If the number is bigger than the dial, the needle just goes around again and lands where it should. A thousand on the dial would look like no speedometer anyone has ever seen, so the dial stays five hundred and the needle does the laps. Two readings of one truth, never two truths.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Your score is the big number at the top. The round dial underneath is just a picture of that same number — it always points where the number says. If the number is bigger than the dial, the needle goes all the way around and comes back to where it should land, like going around a racetrack one more time. The picture never disagrees with the number, because the number is the boss.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the big number and the little dial finally agree, love — the dial just follows the number now, dear, going round again when it needs to and landing right where it should. No more two different answers, love. One truth, told twice.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is a definition, not a fix: the gauge is defined as a picture of the featured number. Before this decision the gauge and the tiles were two independent readings that happened to disagree (83% vs 52%, different totals), and the question was which one to change. His answer removes the question entirely — there is only one reading, and the gauge renders it. The 500 dial is a realism constraint from his eye (no speedometer reads to a thousand), and the lap rule is the mechanism that keeps a 500 dial honest above 500. Any future gauge that disagrees with its number is now wrong by definition, not by taste — and the test is one line: does the needle land where the number says?

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE % MISMATCH IS CLOSED:** 83% tiles vs 52% gauge is settled — the gauge follows the featured number in every mode.
- **THE DIAL STAYS 500:** a 1000 dial was considered and rejected as unrealistic for a speedometer.
- **THE LAP RULE:** needle laps the dial in sets of 500 and lands at the remainder (777 → one lap, lands 277).
- **THE DEFINITION:** the number is the truth; the gauge is its picture. A gauge that disagrees with its number is wrong by definition.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A dashboard that shows two different values for the same thing teaches the reader not to trust either one. The mismatch sat open all day because it looked like a math problem — which total is right? — when it was really a definition problem: which reading is the truth? Shawn answered the definition, and the math problem disappears with it. Every gauge on every page now has the same law to follow, and the next time a needle and a number disagree, the fix is known before anyone asks: make the needle follow the number.

The orb rule is the digit-color law applied to orbs (each its own color, none the same), and the mode-pill rule is the same law applied to controls (three separate icons, each lighting in its own color). The fold-away rule is a new behavior law: chrome that is sticky while using the app is chrome that is in the way. The test for all of it is his eye on the rendered viewport — which is SN-2508.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The Dashboard is the first of the four core pages and the one he looks at most. A hero that fights its own chrome teaches the reader that the page is not finished, no matter how good the numbers are. These orders are small — a fold here, a color there — but together they are the difference between a page that presents and a page that crowds. And they were all visible in one screenshot, which is why the checking rule (SN-2508) matters as much as the fixes: the defects were obvious to his eye the moment he looked.

- **THE REBUKE:** the checks were passing numbers while the page looked messy to his eye. The orbs were one color, crashed into the gauge, the big orb covering the number tiles, the mode strip one flat bar — and the checks passed anyway. A verification that cannot see mess is not verification.
- **THE RULE, NOW STANDING:** verification means looking at the rendered viewpoint the way he sees it. Seats judge screenshots like a human eye, not just rects and bytes. If the page looks messy by eye, it fails — whatever the numbers said.
- **WHAT IT REPLACES:** measurement-only verification. Rects, contrast ratios, byte counts, and popup checks are preparation, never proof. They catch what they are told to catch; the eye catches what nobody told it to look for.
- **WHAT IT DOES NOT REPLACE:** the measurements still run — they are the preparation. But no work moves on measurements alone. The viewpoint check is the gate the work passes through, and his eye is the final gate after that.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Imagine a building inspector who measures every wall with a laser and declares the house perfect — while the front door is hanging off its hinges in plain sight. The measurements were right; the house was still wrong, because nobody looked at it. Shawn's rule is the look: before anything is called done, someone looks at the actual page the way he looks at it, on his screen, and asks — is this messy? If yes, it fails, no matter what the instruments said. The instruments prepare the work; the eye judges it.

layers.body: If you clean your room by measuring it with a ruler but never looking at it, you might miss the big pile of toys in the middle of the floor. The ruler says the room is tidy. Your eyes say it isn't. From now on, we always look at the room with our eyes before we say it's clean — the looking is the real check.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the numbers said it was fine and his eyes said it was messy, love — and the eyes were right, dear. From now on we look at the thing itself, with our own eyes, before we call it done. A ruler can't see a mess, love. Eyes can.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is the verification law catching up with the Live Viewpoint Method: no seat scorecard or verification is proof; only his eye is. SN-2508 makes that operational for every seat — the viewpoint check is not an extra step, it is THE check, and it happens before anything is reported done. It also explains the failure mode of the whole morning: seats verified mechanics (popups, padding, contrast, rects) and never asked whether the page looked right, so obvious defects — orbs crashed into the gauge, a flat mode bar, tabs eating the hero — walked past scout, rebuild, two verifiers, and the captain's browser check. The rule is cheap to apply (look at the screenshot as a human would) and it would have caught every one of them. A check that cannot fail on mess cannot pass on quality.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE VIEWPOINT IS THE CHECK:** every verification looks at the rendered viewpoint the way he sees it — desktop + phone, scroll 0 AND scrolled.
- **MESSY BY EYE IS A FAIL:** a pass on numbers that looks messy by eye is a fail, full stop.
- **MEASUREMENT IS PREPARATION:** rects, bytes, and contrast ratios still run — but they are never the proof on their own.
- **HIS EYE IS THE FINAL GATE:** the seat's eye-check prepares the work; his eye decides it.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Every defect in SN-2507 was visible in a single screenshot. The reason they shipped is not that the builders were careless — it is that the verification asked the wrong question. "Do the numbers pass?" is a question a machine can answer, and the machine answered yes while the page was messy. "Does it look right?" is a question only an eye can answer, and nobody asked it. This note changes the question every seat asks before reporting done. It is the cheapest fix in the system — one look — and it is the one that would have caught the most defects.

The four core pages run in order — Dashboard first, then Personal, then Hub, then Pricing — each finished and proven before the next, and MAXESS rides immediately behind Dashboard.

His two words — "Not yet" — save that whole branch of work from being built on an unmade decision. And the order itself is the strategy: Dashboard first means his attention, the seats' attention, and the verification all land on one page until it is done, instead of spreading across two.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He asked a simple question — how many of these can I actually click into? — and got a confident wrong answer, because the count came from a checklist that stopped at 28 rows and never looked at the other 8. The re-audit did the honest thing: it checked every row by its bytes, and the answer nearly doubled, from 10 to 18. And when you open a toy, you want to see the whole thing, not peek at it through a tiny window — full page, with just an X to close it.

That is the pricing page's lesson in miniature: the words are largely settled, and what remains is making sure the reader's eye lands where it should, in the order it should. And the buried-section law applies to every page, not just this one — if he can't find it, it isn't there.

notes.title: One Deploy Shape — Or Every Fix Dies at the Next Sync
notes.subtitle: In the 24 hours to 2026-11-09 06:37 Vancouver time, the /s/ short-link fix landed (PR #3301), was click-proven closed, and was then overwritten by the Smart Notes sync, which redeploys the Hub through a raw upload carrying no bindings — wiping the worker's bindings and serving an old shell. The root cause was proven three ways, the sync's own deployer was rebuilt to build from the repo's HUB/ source, and worker behaviour survived a sync deploy for the first time. The same day, the Intelligence Loop kept filing notes at a pace no registry could follow — 212 commits, 205 distinct Smart Notes filed, while Project Intelligence stayed flat at 30 proven out of 660 — and two notes collided on the same numbers (SN-2482, SN-2483) and were healed by renumbering. Together: the system does not lack effort or even fixes. It lacks one deploy shape, one registry that keeps up, and one proof standard that counts only what survives and what a person can open.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: When two machines write to the same place in different ways, the last one wins and the first one's work disappears — silently. The cure is not more care. The cure is one way of writing, used by everyone, every time. The same is true for the notes: filing them faster than they are registered does not build a brain, it builds a bigger pile that is harder to search. Speed counts only when the catalog, the feed, and the reader keep up with it.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: If you fix the door and then a robot comes along and puts the old broken door back — every single night — the fix is not to fix the door faster. The fix is to teach the robot to use the new door.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It is like two cooks seasoning the same pot without talking. Each one undoes the other. You do not need better cooks. You need one recipe card on the wall that both of them follow.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Evidence from this window: board receipts 6725477204 (diagnosis), 6726245900 (first closing, click-proven), 6727766154 (root cause closed — the sync's bindings-less raw PUT, Cloudflare audit times 19:32–20:57Z, 2026-11-08), and the 2026-11-08 learning-event filing (PR #3304) recording that Nitro's fixed deployer landed 23:05Z and worker behaviour survived a sync deploy for the first time, with closure still pending two consecutive browser LIVE checks. SN-2503, filed in this same window, carries the twin lesson in its title: "Synced Is Not Live." This note itself is filed in GitHub by PR and is NOT claimed live — its registry and feed steps, and its life in NayaNET, are still owed.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- Every automated writer to a live surface must use the same deploy shape as the surface's own builder — one recipe, or the overwrites continue.
- A closing claim needs proof that survives the next automated cycle, not just proof at the moment of the fix.
- Filing pace is not intelligence pace: 205 notes filed in a day with a registry gap in the hundreds is intake outrunning the brain.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The /s/ links were Shawn's named single priority on 2026-11-08. They were genuinely fixed — and the system itself undid the fix. Until there is one deploy shape, every future fix to the Hub carries the same hidden expiry date, and every "problem solved" receipt is provisional whether it says so or not.

notes.title: The Unstick — State Surgery Works, and Two Keys Disagreeing Is the Cause

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: A letter was stamped "delivered" and never arrived, and the fix was not to stamp it again — it was to cross one line out of the book so the postman would pick the letter up again. The book and the mailbox disagreed about what exists, and nobody had ever made them agree. The repair took three minutes once someone looked at both. The lesson is not the three minutes — it is that two lists that never check each other will always, eventually, disagree, and the disagreement will always look like nothing is wrong.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine your big brother's notebook says your drawing was delivered, but the drawing is still in the mailbox. The fix is simple: erase that one line from his notebook, and he will pick the drawing up and deliver it for real. Then go and look at your friend's doorstep to make sure it arrived. Erasing the line is not cheating — it is telling the notebook the truth.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the letter got there in the end, love — all it took was crossing out the one wrong line in the book, dear, so the postman would carry it again. Two lists that never check each other will always disagree one day, love, and the only cure is to look at the doorstep yourself, dear. That's the whole of it: erase the wrong line, carry the letter, and check the doorstep, dear.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: This is SN-2503 with its proof attached. SN-2503 said the state can mask a stuck note and named the fix shape before it was tried: a manual feed build + Hub redeploy, or a state reset for that one path. The captain chose the state reset, and it worked in one pass — 154 seconds, two notes synced, feed 591 → 593. The new knowledge is the mechanism: the state is keyed on the file-fetch sha and the feed build on the tree listing, and a pass where the two disagree strands the card with no re-trigger. That is a class, not an incident — any system with two sources of "what exists" and no reconciliation read will do this again. The cure is now a procedure any seat can run. The prevention is still owed: the sync must verify the feed contains what it synced, or the redeploy failure must surface somewhere durable. Until then, the loop's live check is the only reconciliation the machine has — and this run is the proof it works: the stuck note was found, the fix was named, the fix was tried, the bytes prove it landed.
