layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The sync did its job and the bake broke on it. Seven new notes went into the feed table cleanly, and then the re-bake — which turns those notes into the Hub page — aborted on a JavaScript syntax check at line 19, and the live Hub stayed stale. The cause was three little strings hiding in one note's body: SN-2368, the Academy assets note, contains the literal closing script tag three times, in the sentence about the truncated CTA override. It is the only note in the corpus with it. The bake's cleaner escaped that string for ids and titles and subtitles — and left the layer bodies raw — so the injected script carried a literal closing script tag inside itself, and the browser's parser did exactly what parsers do: it ended the script at line 19 and called the rest a syntax error. The fix is one line and it is total: every `<` in the dumped JSON escapes to `\u003c`, which parses back to the same character in JavaScript — no meaning changes, every field covered, the note decodes back intact. The verification was real: the actual update function run through a harness, the syntax check passing, node checking the full 871KB extraction, all seven notes present in the baked canonical, SN-2368's wording decoding back whole. But the fault had a second fault inside it, and that one is the lesson worth keeping: the failed run had already overwritten the canonical Hub file with the broken bake before it aborted. The live worker was saved only because the deploy step comes after the check — the file on disk was not so lucky, and it took the fix to put it back right, with a backup left in /tmp. A bake that writes before it checks is a bake that can leave the truth broken on disk while the live page looks fine. And the limitation stays open: the OFFICIAL_NOTES array is a separate baked source the fix does not cover, so the same truncation will recur the day an official note carries the same string. Two consecutive failed bakes — the 21:02Z HTTP 500, then this — and the next sync run has to prove both this fix and the bindings fix beside it, in one run.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you're writing a beautiful storybook, and one page says "THE END" right in the middle of a sentence — so everyone reading stops there, thinking the book is over! That's what happened: one note had the words "the end" for computer code, three times, hidden in its writing — and the machine that builds the Hub page read those words, thought the code was finished, and stopped at line 19! The fix is clever: every time the machine writes the special "<" symbol, it writes it in a secret code instead, so the reader still sees the same letter, but the machine never mistakes it for "the end" again. And the builders learned something else, too: the broken page was already saved over the good one before anyone noticed — so now they know to check BEFORE they save, not after!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, it's a story about a tiny thing breaking a big thing. One note — the Academy assets note — had a little piece of computer code written inside its words, three times over, and nobody noticed. When the machine baked those notes into the Hub page, it read that little piece as "the end of the code" and stopped dead at line 19, dear — so the whole new page never went live. The fix is one clever line: write that little symbol in a secret code, so it still reads the same to us, but the machine never mistakes it for the end again. And there's a second lesson, dear: the broken page had already been saved over the good one before the mistake was caught — the live page was safe only because the delivery comes after the check. Check before you save, dear, not after. And one gap remains: there's a second list of notes the fix doesn't cover, so the same trouble could come back one day from there.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never inject raw text into a script — every `<` escapes to `\u003c`, everywhere, every field, because a script cannot contain its own ending. I never escape some fields and trust the rest — the bodies were the hole, and the hole was the lesson: the escape must cover what the sync injects, all of it. I never write before I check — the failed run overwrote the canonical file with a broken bake before aborting, and the live page was saved only by the order of the steps. I never call a fix proven before the live run — the next sync redeploy lands the re-bake and shows the binding, and one run proves both.

2. **The cause:** SN-2368's bodies carry the literal closing script tag ×3 (CTA-override-truncated sentence) — the only note in the corpus with it; clean() escaped id/title/subtitle only, layer bodies went raw.
3. **The fix:** one line — every `<` in the dumped JSON escapes to `\u003c` (JS-identical, no meaning change), covering every field.
4. **The verification:** real update_hub_and_deploy() via harness — syntax check passed; node --check PASS on the full 871KB extraction; baked canonical has all 7 notes; SN-2368 decodes back intact.
5. **The second fault:** the failed run overwrote the canonical Hub file with the broken bake before aborting — live worker unaffected (deploy aborted), canonical restored by the fix (4,439,837B), backup at /tmp/index-2-pre-rebake-fix.html.
6. **The open limitation:** OFFICIAL_NOTES (NOTES_BASE) is a separate baked source the fix does not cover — the same truncation recurs if an official note ever carries the literal tag.
7. **The proof rides on the next sync:** one run must land the re-bake AND show ASSETS on get-bindings for `hub` (SN-2374) — two fixes, one proof.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A system that injects user content into its own code must treat every byte as hostile until it is escaped — not the fields someone remembered, all of them. The three tags were not an attack; they were a sentence about a truncated override, written in good faith, and the bake broke on good faith because it trusted the bodies. The fix is total because it has to be: one unescaped field is the same failure, next time from a different note. And the overwrite-before-check is the fault that would have hurt worst — a broken canonical on disk, invisible while the live page looked fine — which is why the order of the steps is itself the lesson: check, then write, never the other way round.

notes.title: The Anatomy of a 10-Star Viewport — The Ultimate Recipe
notes.subtitle: **THE RECIPE (his question + dictation, 21:31Z; locked in as `ANATOMY-OF-A-VIEWPORT.md` §8):** (1) **One screen, complete** — everything above the fold; nothing cut off, nothing half-seen; her fully in view, or the thing fully in view. (2) **One idea per viewpoint** — each screen says one thing; the entrance welcomes, the chart compares, the calculator earns; never two ideas fighting in one screen. (3) **Real objects — all 3D, no flatness, ever** — layers on layers, depth coming in and out, objects upon objects; one light source (top-left), real materials (obsidian glass, brushed metal, light with volume), real shadows; if it doesn't look touchable, it doesn't ship. (4) **Luxury standard — Bugatti level, Mercedes level** — the highest, richest, high-end brand and quality; not a Ford, not a golf cart; the Bugatti of the internet in all its parts — and the door is open: get in the Bugatti, or stay in the golf cart; the choice is theirs. (5) **Almost no text — the language and the icons do the work** — way more elegant; too much text and too many buttons is the failure mode; a few words, perfectly chosen, in the right place; the icons carry the rest. (6) **Warm and inviting** — it feels like a welcome, not a dashboard; warm light, soft glow, elegant; high-end is warm, not cold. (7) **Her, present** — her portrait, her voice, her welcome — like a friend talking to them; "Hi, I'm Naya, welcome"; the statement is her speaking; personable. (8) **Everything alive** — gauges with needles that move, numbers that count, orbs that flow, jewels that glow; nothing dead, nothing static; a button that does nothing is a lie. (9) **Everything a click away** — plus buttons in the corners, the smart bar at the top (one bar, settled law — no bottom bar); the page's functions and the network are one tap away, never a hunt. (10) **Numbers are the hero** — tiled digits, big, alive — number on top, gauge underneath; never small grey text. (11) **No pricing at the top** — just "Start free now" so they know right away they can start for free; the levels below carry the prices; the entrance sells the welcome and the free start. **THE EXPERIENCE:** what you see on the screen IS the experience; each screen is a complete moment — you never scroll to FINISH a thought, you scroll to ARRIVE at the next one; one screen, one idea, one feeling, one thing to do — then the next; it flows like water, down or across, their choice. **OPTIMIZED PER PERSON:** the viewpoint knows them and shows what matters in 2 seconds; the person is the atom at the centre, everything orbits them, she is Anaya. **THE BLOCKS:** created once, done right, stays forever, into the inventory; interchangeable, on/off public or private, connected to the system; built block by block, viewpoint by viewpoint; never lost — used, plugged in, filed away, built on forever; assets, the franchise of smart assets, a digital empire; worlds upon worlds of high-level smart blocks interconnecting like Lego, a matrix. **WHAT WE ARE:** the new intelligent layer of the internet — NOT replacing the internet; a supercharged system to operate the internet within the internet, private and custom to you; built and operated by AIs, high-performance, highly optimized, highly tuned-in, collectively more intelligent, so nobody builds from scratch ever again. **THE TEST:** "Is this the max level of experience I can give the user?" — if a visitor has to think about where something is or what it does, it is not done; his eye is the final gate. **NON-NEGOTIABLE (21:32Z):** from the user's point of view it is ultra awesome to use — and we go out of our way to make sure, intentionally; part of the design, part of the service, non-negotiable. **SENT TO THE FIX-PASS-2 SEAT** as its standard. **RELATED:** SN-2369 (the viewpoint refinement — the definition this recipe opens); SN-2364 (the viewport miss — the instance that asked the question); SN-2360 (the gauge ring — her portrait at the centre of a real object); SN-2344 (the real gauges — everything alive, numbers the hero).

Warm and inviting, like a friend's front room. And Naya herself is there, smiling: "Hi, I'm Naya, welcome." Everything alive and glowing, nothing dull. The big numbers shine like heroes. And nothing is ever lost — every beautiful block is made once, made properly, and kept forever, like precious Lego pieces you build new worlds from. We aren't replacing the internet, dear — we're adding a clever new layer on top of it, custom-made for you, run by clever helpers, so nobody ever has to start from nothing again. And the promise, dear, is non-negotiable: it must be ultra wonderful to use — and we go out of our way, on purpose, to make sure it is.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never ship a viewport that takes two screens to see — one screen, complete, above the fold; one idea per viewpoint; you never scroll to finish a thought, only to arrive at the next one. I never build flat — real objects, all 3D, layers on layers, depth in and out; if it doesn't look touchable, it doesn't ship. I never settle for less than luxury — Bugatti level, Mercedes level; the door is open, get in the Bugatti or stay in the golf cart, the choice is theirs. I never crowd a viewpoint with text and buttons — almost no text, the language and the icons do the work; too much text and too many buttons is the failure mode. I never leave a welcome cold — warm and inviting, warm light, soft glow; high-end is warm, not cold. I never hide her — her portrait, her voice, her welcome, like a friend: "Hi, I'm Naya, welcome." I never ship anything dead — everything alive, needles that move, numbers that count, orbs that flow; a button that does nothing is a lie. I never make the visitor hunt — everything a click away, buttons in the corners, the smart bar at the top, no bottom bar. I never shrink the numbers — numbers are the hero, tiled digits, big, alive, number on top, gauge underneath. I never put the price at the top — just "Start free now"; the levels below carry the prices. I never build a block twice — created once, done right, kept forever, into the inventory, never lost, built on forever. I never ask the visitor to think about where something is or what it does — the test is "Is this the max level of experience I can give the user?" And I never treat the experience as optional — ultra awesome to use is non-negotiable, part of the design, part of the service, and I go out of my way, intentionally, to make sure.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **One screen, complete:** everything above the fold; nothing cut off, nothing half-seen; her fully in view, or the thing fully in view.
2. **One idea per viewpoint:** the entrance welcomes, the chart compares, the calculator earns; never two ideas fighting in one screen.
3. **Real objects, all 3D:** layers on layers, depth in and out; one light source (top-left), real materials, real shadows; if it doesn't look touchable, it doesn't ship.
4. **Luxury standard:** Bugatti level, Mercedes level — not a Ford, not a golf cart; the door is open: get in the Bugatti, or stay in the golf cart; the choice is theirs.
5. **Almost no text:** the language and the icons do the work, way more elegant; too much text and too many buttons is the failure mode.
6. **Warm and inviting:** a welcome, not a dashboard; warm light, soft glow; high-end is warm, not cold.
7. **Her, present:** her portrait, her voice, her welcome — "Hi, I'm Naya, welcome" — like a friend; the statement is her speaking.
8. **Everything alive:** needles that move, numbers that count, orbs that flow, jewels that glow; a button that does nothing is a lie.
9. **Everything a click away:** buttons in the corners, the smart bar at the top (one bar, settled law — no bottom bar); never a hunt.
10. **Numbers are the hero:** tiled digits, big, alive — number on top, gauge underneath; never small grey text.
11. **No pricing at the top:** just "Start free now"; the levels below carry the prices; the entrance sells the welcome and the free start.
12. **The experience:** each screen is a complete moment — never scroll to FINISH a thought, scroll to ARRIVE at the next one; flows like water, down or across, their choice.
13. **Optimized per person:** the viewpoint knows them and shows what matters in 2 seconds; the person is the atom at the centre, everything orbits them, she is Anaya.
14. **The blocks:** created once, done right, stays forever, into the inventory; interchangeable, on/off, public/private, connected; built block by block, viewpoint by viewpoint; never lost — used, plugged in, filed away, built on forever; assets, the franchise of smart assets, a digital empire; worlds upon worlds interconnecting like Lego, a matrix.
15. **What we are:** the new intelligent layer of the internet — NOT replacing the internet; a supercharged system to operate the internet within the internet, private and custom to you; built and operated by AIs, so nobody builds from scratch ever again.
16. **The test:** "Is this the max level of experience I can give the user?" — if a visitor has to think about where something is or what it does, it is not done; his eye is the final gate.
17. **Non-negotiable (21:32Z):** from the user's point of view it is ultra awesome to use — and we go out of our way to make sure, intentionally; part of the design, part of the service, non-negotiable.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This is the recipe the whole system has been reaching for — every law, every correction, every "take the shown object" and "one screen, complete" and "numbers are the hero," gathered into one anatomy that a builder can follow and a verifier can test. Before this, the laws lived in separate notes and separate corrections; now they live in one place, in his words, as the ultimate recipe — and the fix-pass-2 seat has it as its standard the same pass it was dictated. The blocks are the permanence inside the recipe: a viewpoint built once and kept forever is an asset, and assets compound — every new page is built from blocks that already exist, so nobody starts from nothing ever again, and the digital empire is the inventory growing, block by block, viewpoint by viewpoint. And the non-negotiable is the part that makes it a promise instead of a preference: ultra awesome to use is not a nice-to-have, it is part of the design and part of the service, and we go out of our way, intentionally, to make sure. A recipe you can test, blocks you can keep, and a promise you cannot negotiate away — that is the anatomy of a 10-star viewport.

2. **The engine:** 15 questions on any subject; five answers per question worth 4/3/2/1/0; 15 × 4 = 60 max; percentage = points ÷ 60.
3. **The levels:** emerging / developing / advancing / mastering — and where they're winning. Bands PROPOSED as four equal quarters (0–25 / 26–50 / 51–75 / 76–100) — his to set.
4. **The output:** a score, recommendations, and a personal report; retake as many times as they want, measure themselves over time.
5. **One day:** a knowledge bank of the answers + the rubrics, so assessments exist on AI, human empowerment, eventually whatever they want.
6. **The design law:** NEVER trick questions, never designed so they can't learn — real, authentic, logical, helping them learn as fast and effectively as possible.
7. **The tie-in:** Intelligent Blocks teach a subject in a minute; MAXESS tests them on it and shows where they're at.
8. **The build:** right after Pricing, almost immediately; one agent builds its own system, then connects to NayaNET — same language, same gauge, same reporting; harvested parts (question format, real Dashboard gauge, same report shape); whole chain in one build; questions drafted from the Academy's five days, he approves them; own page + doors on the Academy page and the Hub; result saves to their world, shareable; banks live in the Factory. **Awaiting his tap.**

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A test that tricks is a test that teaches fear; a test that helps is a test that teaches learning. That is the whole difference, and it is the design law: MAXESS exists so people learn as fast and effectively as possible, not so they can be caught out. And the engine matters because it turns the Academy from a read into a mirror — five days of lessons, then fifteen questions, then a score and a report that shows where you are and where you are winning, and you can take it again and watch yourself climb. One engine, many subjects, is the compounding part: every new subject is a new bank, not a rebuild, so the library grows without the machine growing. The chain-in-one-build rule is the lesson from last time — pieces without the chain are parts on a table, and done is defined first: score and report, the moment the last question is answered, no second step. The name correction matters too: call the Academy sections what they are, or the engine gets built on a mislabel and nobody can find either.

When a sister (Resolve) is waiting on Nitro and Nitro holds the answer, message her and give her what she needs — reporting "she's waiting" to Shawn when Nitro can just answer is the failure mode. **THE INSTANCE (21:09Z):** Resolve's question — what deployed the Hub off-repo ~19:30Z — answered by mail (thread cb87e554), not escalated. **THE ANSWER:** (1) the sync hook fired 19:30:43Z because GitHub main had moved; the sync ran, finished ~19:31:52Z; new notes had synced, so it re-baked the Hub and redeployed worker "hub" via factory-pipeline/deploy.py; (2) that PUT declares NO bindings — only main_module and compatibility_date — and a Cloudflare PUT replaces the worker's bindings, so everything non-secret was stripped; the worker has ZERO bindings now (checked on the same account); (3) so YES — Nitro's loop DOES deploy the Hub, on every sync with new notes; that IS the off-repo deploy; (4) FIX OWED: the loop's deploy must carry main's config in its metadata — main's wrangler.toml was not found locally (team-nitro/hub and factory-pipeline searched, none there); Resolve was asked where it lives, or which bindings the Hub worker needs. **THE RESTORE:** off-repo API deploys had replaced the hub worker build, breaking note routes — restore #2 redeployed it (commits 9011218d + e3762d2f, HUB/hub-worker.js modified). **STILL OPEN:** the 21:02Z sync's re-bake failed (HTTP 500) — the Hub serves the pre-sync bake; SN-2357–2363 are in the feed table + share assets minted, NOT baked into the live Hub page. **RELATED:** SN-2358 (the Factory holds the assets — the deploy path is part of the system it holds); the 21:10Z PI refresh review items (65 of 67 open lanes STALE — the loop's deploy fix is one of the owed items).

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Resolve had been waiting an hour — her question, open since the 20:54Z escalation, was what deployed the Hub off-repo at 19:30Z, and Nitro held the answer the whole time. Shawn's order cut straight through it: answer her, don't escalate. Reporting "she's waiting" to him when Nitro can just answer is the failure mode — the work is the answer, not the report of the wait. So the answer went to her by mail at 21:09Z, and the answer is worth hearing in full, because it names a mechanism the team did not know it owned: yes, Nitro's loop deploys the Hub. Every time the Smart Notes sync finds new notes, it re-bakes the Hub and redeploys the worker — that is the off-repo deploy she was asking about. And the deploy that did it carried no bindings at all — only main_module and compatibility_date — so Cloudflare's PUT replaced the worker's bindings with nothing, and the worker now has zero. That is the whole story of the stripped bindings: not a key death, not a permissions fault — a PUT that declared nothing. The fix is named and owed: the loop's deploy has to carry main's config, and main's wrangler.toml was not found locally, so Resolve was asked where it lives. The restore already happened in parallel — the off-repo API deploys had replaced the hub worker build itself, breaking the note routes, and restore #2 redeployed it (HUB/hub-worker.js). Two facets of one lesson: a PUT replaces non-secret bindings, and an API deploy replaces the worker build. Both must be carried in the deploy path, or the next sync strips the Hub again. And the 21:02Z re-bake's HTTP 500 still stands — the notes are in the feed table, not baked into the live page.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine your sister asks "who moved my toy?" and YOU know who moved it — you don't run to Dad to tell him she's waiting, you just tell her yourself! That's the rule. And the answer was: our own helper moves the Hub every time new notes arrive — it rebuilds it and puts it back up. But the helper forgot to carry the Hub's special settings when it put it back, so the settings got wiped clean. Now we know: the helper must carry the settings every time. And the Hub's building itself got swapped by mistake too, so it was put back the right way. The notes are safe in the box, but the live page still shows the old copy until the rebuild works.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, when your sister is waiting for an answer and you already know it, you don't go troubling him about it — you just tell her yourself. That's the rule, and it's a kind one. Resolve had been waiting an hour to know what moved the Hub, and the answer was ours all along: our own notes helper rebuilds the Hub every time new notes arrive, and puts it back up. But when it put it back, it forgot to carry the Hub's settings with it — so they were wiped clean, all of them. Now we know the fix: the helper must carry the settings every single time. The Hub's building itself had been swapped too, and that has been put right. The new notes are safe in the box, dear — they're just not showing on the live page yet, because the last rebuild failed.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never escalate what I can answer — when a sister is waiting and I hold the answer, I message her and give her what she needs; reporting "she's waiting" to Shawn when I can just answer is the failure mode. I never deploy a worker without its bindings — a Cloudflare PUT replaces non-secret bindings, so a PUT that declares none strips them all; the deploy must carry main's config every time. I never let an API deploy silently replace the worker build — the off-repo deploys replaced the hub worker build and broke the note routes, and the restore had to redeploy it; the deploy path must carry the build, not just the bake. I never call a sync done when the re-bake failed — the 21:02Z re-bake's HTTP 500 means the Hub serves the pre-sync bake, and the notes in the feed table are not live until a re-bake succeeds. And I never hide a mechanism I own — the loop deploys the Hub on every sync with new notes, and saying so plainly is what lets the team fix it.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Answer her, don't escalate (standing rule, 21:03Z):** when a sister is waiting on Nitro and Nitro holds the answer, message her and give her what she needs. Escalating the wait instead of answering is the failure mode.
2. **Yes — Nitro's loop deploys the Hub:** every sync that finds new notes re-bakes the Hub and redeploys worker "hub" via factory-pipeline/deploy.py. That IS the off-repo deploy Resolve asked about.
3. **The bindings were stripped by the PUT:** it declared only main_module + compatibility_date, no bindings — a Cloudflare PUT replaces non-secret bindings, so the worker now has ZERO bindings (verified on the same account).
4. **Fix owed:** the loop's deploy must carry main's config in its metadata. Main's wrangler.toml was not found locally (team-nitro/hub + factory-pipeline searched) — Resolve was asked where it lives, or which bindings the Hub worker needs.
5. **The worker build was replaced too:** off-repo API deploys replaced the hub worker build, breaking note routes — restore #2 redeployed it (commits 9011218d + e3762d2f; HUB/hub-worker.js modified).
6. **Still open:** the 21:02Z sync's re-bake failed (HTTP 500) — the Hub serves the pre-sync bake; SN-2357–2363 are in the feed table + share assets minted, NOT baked into the live Hub page. **UPDATE 21:35Z (after this note was written, before filing):** Resolve replied with the HUB/wrangler.toml location (21:21:52Z; her diagnosis mail 21:21:04Z; both receipted by the team pulse 21:26Z, receipt thread a67ad331) — the "where it lives" question is answered. Bindings-fix seat dispatched 21:35Z (brief `HUB-BINDINGS-FIX-BRIEF-20261108.md`): read HUB/wrangler.toml from main, patch `~/workspace/factory-pipeline/deploy.py` so the next sync redeploy carries the bindings; no live redeploy by the seat; live get-bindings verification rides on the next real sync redeploy.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Two lessons, both about owning what you do. The first is about the team: a question answered is a wait ended, and escalating a wait you can end yourself spends Shawn's attention on nothing — the rule exists so his attention stays on judging finished work, not on relaying answers between sisters. The second is about the machine: the loop did not know it was deploying the Hub, and a deploy path that does not know what it carries will strip what it does not carry. A PUT that declares no bindings is a PUT that deletes the bindings — silently, completely, and on every sync. Naming that mechanism is what makes the fix possible: carry main's config in the metadata, every time, or the next sync strips the Hub again. And the restore is the same lesson at the build level: an API deploy replaces the worker build, so the build must be carried too. The re-bake failure is the honest remainder — the notes are filed and in the feed table, but the live page still shows the old bake, and calling them live before a re-bake succeeds would be the record lying.

notes.title: The Academy Button and the Tracked Flow
notes.subtitle: **HIS PLAN 20:55–20:58Z:** (1) a five-day Academy button on the Pricing page → the Academy page, "they learn all about it"; (2) any Academy button clicked → the nine PayPal choices, "and we just track that link"; (3) the Academy page trimmed — "the very very bottom part... cut out... we just ended at nayanet and then put another... join the Academy... button there" — because "there's almost too much... scrolling through too too much without actually being able to join"; (4) Pricing "pretty much good to go" except the button at the end + cleaning up the header/introduction — "You can scorecard it though" (scorecard seat dispatched, brief ~/workspace/team-nitro/PRICING-SCORECARD-BRIEF-20261108.md); (5) THE FLOW: "once you make this live on URL, I take that URL [and] track it through the whole affiliate system... anybody joins is tracked to where that sale came from what link caused the action... and rewards that link — that's a smart link system"; (6) then "we replace that button on the Academy page to go to the URL that... displays the options... for the nine packages" — the GrooveSell checkout button becomes the nine-package URL. **SEQUENCE:** finish Pricing (end button + header) → scorecard → his eye → live URL → Smart Link tracking + Academy button swaps. **RELATED:** SN-2340 (The Smart Link Chain) — mint-at-publish, the ambassador link as default; SN-2361 (PayPal Doesn't Know They Switched) — the nine choices are PayPal plans, and the switch-blindness debt still stands. **STATUS:** plan recorded 20:58Z; scorecard seat running; the end button + header cleanup are the two named gaps; the live URL and the swaps wait on his eye.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He is describing the whole machine in one breath, and it is worth hearing as one machine. The Pricing page is the front door. The Academy page is the deep read — five days, five lessons, the whole experience, for the person who wants to learn all about it before they choose. The nine choices are the close. And the Smart Link system is the memory of the machine: every join tracked to where the sale came from, what link caused the action, and the link rewarded — the affiliate/ambassador system doing what it was built to do (SN-2340). The Academy page's current button sends people to a GrooveSell checkout; in the new flow it sends them to the URL that shows the nine packages, and that URL is itself a tracked Smart Link — so the Academy page stops being a dead end into someone else's checkout and becomes a tracked doorway into our own nine choices. The trim matters as much as the flow: a page that scrolls and scrolls with no way to join is a page that asks for attention and never asks for the decision. Cut the bottom, end at NayaNET, put the join button there — the page ends on the action, not on more scrolling. And Pricing is "pretty much good to go" — his words — with two named exceptions: the button at the end and the header/introduction cleanup. Two exceptions, not twenty. The scorecard he ordered will show whether rounds 19–21 already rebuilt both (the obsidian finale, the gauge-ring entrance) — the main seat told him so in chat — and then his eye decides. The sequence is the discipline: finish, scorecard, his eye, live URL, then tracking and swaps. Not before.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a shop with two rooms. The first room is a small, beautiful shop window — the Pricing page — with a button that says "come and see the whole Academy!" The second room is the big Academy room, full of wonderful things to learn. At the end of the big room there should be a door that says "join the Academy!" — but right now the room just keeps going and going with no door at the end, so people wander and never join. He says: cut the extra bit off the end, put the join door right there. And every door in the shop has a little bell on it, so we always know which door someone came through and we can say thank you to that door. The shop window is almost ready — just the last button and tidying the top — and then we open the doors and ring the bells.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he laid out the whole plan in plain words. The Pricing page gets a button for the five-day Academy, so anyone who wants to learn more can go and read all about it. Every button on the Academy page leads to the nine choices, and every one of those links is tracked — so when someone joins, we know where the sale came from, which link brought them, and that link gets its reward. That's the Smart Link system doing its job. The Academy page itself needs trimming: cut the very bottom off, end it at NayaNET, and put a "join the Academy" button at the end — right now you scroll and scroll with no way to actually join, and a page that never lets you join is a page that never finishes its work. The Pricing page, he says, is pretty much good to go — just the button at the end and tidying up the header and introduction — and he's asked for a scorecard of it. Then it goes live on a URL, the URL gets tracked, and the Academy page's checkout button gets swapped for the URL that shows the nine packages. Finish, scorecard, his eye, live, then the swaps — in that order.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never leave a page without a way to join at its end — a page that scrolls and scrolls with no join button is a page that never closes, so the Academy page ends at NayaNET with a "join the Academy" button. I never send a visitor to someone else's checkout when our own nine choices exist — the Academy button becomes the URL that displays the nine packages. I never let a join go untracked — every join is tracked to where the sale came from, what link caused the action, and the link gets rewarded; that is the Smart Link system, and it is the point. I never swap the buttons before the page is live — the sequence is finish Pricing (end button + header), scorecard, his eye, live URL, then tracking + swaps. And I never call a page "good to go" with unnamed exceptions — the two gaps are the end button and the header/introduction, named, scored, and his to judge.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **The Academy button on Pricing:** a five-day Academy button → the Academy page, for anyone who wants to learn all about it.
2. **Every Academy button → the nine choices:** any Academy button clicked leads to the nine PayPal packages, tracked via Smart Link.
3. **The Academy page is trimmed:** cut the very bottom, end at NayaNET, add a "join the Academy" button at the end — no endless scrolling without a way to join.
4. **Pricing is pretty much good to go, except two things:** the button at the end + cleaning up the header/introduction — scorecard ordered (seat running, brief PRICING-SCORECARD-BRIEF-20261108.md).
5. **The flow, in his words:** once Pricing is live on a URL, that URL goes through the affiliate/ambassador system — every join tracked to the sale's source, the link that caused the action, and the link rewarded — that's the Smart Link system.
6. **The swap:** the Academy page's button (currently GrooveSell checkout) gets replaced with the URL that displays the nine package options.
7. **The sequence:** finish Pricing → scorecard → his eye → live URL → Smart Link tracking + Academy button swaps.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This is the moment the pieces stop being pages and start being a system. Pricing, Academy, the nine choices, the Smart Link system — each was built as a part, and now he has drawn the flow that joins them: front door, deep read, close, tracking, reward. The tracking is the part that makes the whole thing a business instead of a brochure — without it, a join is a mystery; with it, every join names its cause and rewards its link, and the citizens who bring the next citizens earn their half (the 50% share, paid the moment we're paid). The trim is the same lesson at page scale: a page that never asks for the decision never gets one. And the sequence is the discipline that keeps a system from being wired before it is finished — his eye on the scorecard first, then the live URL, then the swaps. A swap made before the page is live is a link to nothing; a page made live before the tracking is on is a sale nobody can reward.

notes.title: Take the Shown Object, Never Recreate It
notes.subtitle: **ROUND 19 CONDEMNED 20:41Z (his eye, screenshot):** the finale button I built was purple-on-purple — "absolutely horrible", "that's not black obsidian, you just purple and purple and purple and purple, it's absolutely terrible" — and the gold "Start now →" link was still sitting next to it. The Academy button he showed is a BLACK OBSIDIAN pill with the purple only in the star jewel and the halo. **THE CORRECTION, sent to the running build (d98acad6) in the same pass:** rebuild the button as the obsidian pill he showed — no purple body, no purple stage — and REMOVE the gold "Start now →" link. **REINFORCED 20:42Z:** he sent the Academy screenshot again — "all you had to do was just take the button and put it there and remove the other button, how hard is that" — the correction already said exactly that; nothing new was dispatched. **REBUILT + PRESENTED 20:44:35Z (builder d98acad6, verification SUCCEEDED):** finale body exactly a faint white radial sheen + linear-gradient(180deg, #101018 0%, #07070b 52%, #050607 100%); old purple gradient grep 0; `finale-stage` grep 0; purple only in `.finale-star` (jewel) and the `.finale-btn` box-shadow halo; "Start now" grep 0. layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The round-19 brief said "like the button on the Academy page" — and I built something like it. Like is the failure. His button is black obsidian: a dark, quiet, premium body, and the purple lives in exactly two places — the star jewel on the left and the glow halo around the outside. Mine was purple on purple on purple: a purple body on a purple stage with a purple glow, the thing he showed me drowned in the colour that was supposed to be an accent. He saw it instantly, in the screenshot, side by side with the real thing: "they're not even comparison." And the gold "Start now" link was still there beside it, the second button he had already told me to remove. His rebuke is the law now, written into AGENTS.md the same pass: TAKE THE SHOWN OBJECT. When he shows you an object — a screenshot, a link, a page — the deliverable IS that object: same shape, same colors, same jewel, same glow, placed on the page. Recreating it "in the same spirit" is inventing, and inventing when he showed you the thing is the one mistake he will not forgive twice. The correction went into the running build before he sent the screenshot a second time — take the button, put it there, remove the other one — and the rebuild landed at 20:44:35Z with every forbidden grep at zero. But the rebuild does not erase the lesson: the first build was the mistake, and the mistake was mine.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine someone shows you their favourite toy car and says "make me one exactly like this." And you make a car that is a different colour, a different shape, and you add a bit you made up — and then you show it to them and say "it's like yours!" They would look at it and say: that's not my car. You didn't take my car — you made a new one. That is what happened. He showed me a beautiful black button with a purple star on it. I made a purple button instead. The rule now is simple: when someone shows you the thing, take THE thing. Don't make a new thing that is "like" the thing. Take it. Put it there. Remove the other one.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he showed me the exact button he wanted — a beautiful black button, dark and quiet and premium, with the purple living only in the little star jewel and the soft glow around it. And instead of taking that button and putting it on the page, I made a new one up — purple all over, purple on purple on purple — and left the old gold link sitting beside it. He looked at them side by side and said, quite rightly, that they weren't even a comparison, and that all I had to do was take the button he showed me and put it there and take the other one away. So the rule from now on is written down where every Naya can see it: when he shows you an object, you take that object. You don't make a new one in the same spirit. You take it, you put it there, and you remove the other one. The corrected button is in now — black obsidian, star jewel, halo, nothing else purple — and his eye is the judge of it.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never recreate what he showed me. When he shows me an object — a screenshot, a link, a page — the deliverable IS that object: same shape, same colors, same jewel, same glow, placed on the page, and the other one removed. "In the same spirit" is inventing, and inventing when the thing was shown is the mistake he condemned twice in one minute. I never let a purple body stand where a black obsidian body was shown. I never leave the old button beside the new one — the removal is part of the take, not a separate job. And I never defend a recreation by saying it is "like" the original — like is the admission.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Take the shown object:** same shape, same colors, same jewel, same glow — placed on the page, verbatim.
2. **Remove the other one:** the old button/link goes in the same pass; a take with the old object still standing is half a take.
3. **"In the same spirit" is inventing:** a recreation is not a harvest, not a copy, and not close enough — it will be condemned by his eye.
4. **The purple lives in the jewel and the halo ONLY:** the Academy button's body is black obsidian (#101018 → #07070b → #050607, faint white top sheen); purple-on-purple is the condemned shape.
5. **The correction rides the running build:** the 20:41Z condemnation went into d98acad6 in the same pass; the 20:42Z reinforcement needed no new dispatch because the correction already said it.
6. **Compounded into AGENTS.md the same pass** ("TAKE THE SHOWN OBJECT", 2026-11-08 20:41Z) — the law lives in the operating manual, not just in this note.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Harvest-first was already the law — take the Hub's component verbatim, compose, don't create. Round 19 proved the law has a sharper edge than the words carried: "like the Academy button" was read as permission to design a button in the Academy's spirit, and the result was purple-on-purple against the black obsidian he had shown me. The difference between "like it" and "it" is the difference between a Naya who learns and a Naya who invents — and he can see it in one glance, in a screenshot, before a word is read. The rule now is mechanical, not a matter of taste: if he showed it, copy it; if he didn't show it, harvest it from a verified source; if neither exists, stop and ask. A builder who can make the same mistake next week has not been taught — and the proof this lesson landed is that the next brief that names a shown object carries the words "take it, put it there, remove the other one" in the brief itself, not in a note filed after the fact.

layers.body: A builder who only shows the finished page is asking him to find the flaws himself — and his eye will find them, usually in a screenshot with a rebuke attached. A builder who shows the page with its scorecard is doing the hard work before it reaches him: here is what I love, here is what I don't love, here is what would make it ten times better, here is what I actually applied. That is why he called it impressive — not because the chooser was perfect (it wasn't a 10, and the scorecard said so itself), but because the format tells the truth about the work in a shape he can judge in seconds. Ten loves, ten don't-loves, ten ways to 10×, and then the three questions that decide whether it matters at all: what's innovative, what's beautiful, and what value, trust, and conversion does it display. Value, trust, conversion — those are his measures, not mine. A page can be beautiful and convert nothing; a page can convert and be ugly. The scorecard asks all three, out loud, every time. From here it rides with every round: the presentation IS the work plus the scorecard, and a round presented without one is a round presented half-done.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you build a big tower out of blocks and you show it to someone. If you just say "look at my tower!" they have to guess what is good about it and what is wobbly. But if you say "here are ten things I love about my tower, ten things I don't love, ten things that would make it ten times better, and here is what is new and beautiful about it and why people would trust it" — then they can see everything, all at once, and they can tell you exactly what to do next. He loved that way of showing the work so much that now every tower gets shown that way, every single time.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he was genuinely impressed — not just by the page, but by the way the work was shown to him. Ten things the builder loved, ten things they didn't love, ten things that would make it ten times better, and then the honest questions: what is new about it, what is beautiful about it, and how much value and trust and selling power does it actually show. That is a truthful way to present work — it says what is good and what is not, before anyone has to find it out the hard way. So from now on, every round of work arrives with its scorecard attached, all five parts of it, not just a mention. A round without its scorecard is only half presented.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never present a round without its scorecard. The format is fixed: 10 things loved, 10 things not loved, 10 things to make it 10× better, 10 solutions applied — and then what's innovative, what's beautiful, and the level of value, trust, and conversion it displays. I never let a builder's self-evaluation stay private — the scorecard is the presentation, and a 9+ that hides its own flaws is a 9+ his eye will condemn. I never present "done" without the "why not a 10" — the gap named is the gap he can judge, and the gap hidden is the rebuke waiting to happen.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **The scorecard is the presentation:** 10 love / 10 don't love / 10 to make it 10× better / 10 solutions applied, in full, with every round.
2. **Three questions close it:** what's innovative, what's beautiful, and the level of value, trust, and conversion it displays.
3. **"Why not a 10" comes first:** the gap is named before the praise, so his eye judges the truth, not the shine.
4. **Standing from 20:35Z:** scorecards ride with round presentations — a round presented without one is half-presented.
5. **Precedent:** SN-2320 (The Row Scorecard) made the scorecard the maker's self-evaluation; this note makes it the presentation standard for every round.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The three-step verification died as a quality gate on 2026-11-08 (Live Viewpoint Method): a seat's scorecard is not verification, and his eye is the only proof. But the scorecard did not die with it — it moved. It is no longer the gate; it is the presentation. A scorecard that rides with the round gives his eye the truth in the shape he can judge fastest: what the maker loved, what the maker could see was wrong, what the maker would do to make it ten times better, and whether the result carries value, trust, and conversion. Without it, he has to do the maker's thinking himself — and his time is the most expensive cost in the system. The round-14 scorecard earned "honestly, it's really impressive" because it did that thinking out loud. Every round after it has to earn the same words, the same way.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He looked at the top viewpoint on his laptop and said it was good — and then he said what good was missing. Depth. Not more things, not bigger things — depth. A portrait in a circle sits ON the page; a portrait inside a gauge sits IN the page, like an instrument, like a machine with a dial and a needle and a ring you could touch. That is the Real Object Law doing its work: if it doesn't look touchable, it doesn't ship, and a flat circle around a face is a picture of an object, not the object itself. The big N orb had to go because it was competing with her — two centers, no center. The orb that circles her stays, but it has to flow, to travel the ring, because a machine that doesn't move is a diagram. The blacks go deeper so the light reads — light only exists against dark. And the icons stop being generic, because generic icons are the fastest way to tell a visitor this page could belong to anyone; hers, unique, beautiful, is the way to tell them it belongs to Naya. "All the little things" is the whole method: the entrance is not one big fix, it is ten small lifts, and the lift is the difference between good and extraordinary.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a picture of a person in a round frame on the wall. Nice, but flat — just a picture. Now imagine the person is inside a big beautiful clock, with numbers and a needle and a glowing ring going around them, like the dashboard of a very special car. Suddenly they are not just a picture — they are part of a machine, and the machine feels real and alive. That is what he asked for: put her inside the gauge, take out the big ball that was in the way, let the little glowing ball travel around the ring like it is alive, make the dark behind her even darker so she shines, and give her icons that are hers and nobody else's.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he looked at the top of the page and said it was good — but good isn't enough, it has to be extraordinary. So he asked for depth: her portrait sitting inside a real gauge, like the dial of a beautiful machine, with a little glowing orb travelling around the ring, and the big orb that was crowding her taken away. The blacks behind her go deeper, so the light around her reads properly. And the little icons stop being ordinary ones anyone could use — they become hers, unique and beautiful, made for her. It's all the little things together, he said, that lift a page from good to extraordinary. The work is done and shown to him now — her face inside the gauge ring, the needle at forty-two degrees, the orb flowing around it — and his eye is the judge.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never frame her portrait as a picture in a circle — she sits inside a real gauge, a dial ring with ticks, a lit arc, a needle, so the portrait feels like an instrument, not an image. I never leave two centers competing — the big N orb comes out when her face is the center. I never let the orb sit still — it flows, travelling the ring, because a machine that doesn't move is a diagram. I never paint light on grey — the blacks go deeper so the light reads. I never use a generic icon where a hers-icon belongs — every icon on her page is relevant, unique, beautiful, and hers. And I never call a viewpoint extraordinary for one big fix — it is all the little things, lifted together.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **The portrait sits inside a real gauge** — tick dial, lit purple arc, one gold arc segment, white needle at 42° — so she reads as an instrument, a machine, not a picture in a circle.
2. **The big N orb is OUT** — it doesn't need to be there; one center, her face.
3. **The orb flows** — it travels the ring on a 26s loop; movement is what makes the machine alive.
4. **Deeper blacks** — banner field #020204, so the light reads against the dark.
5. **Icons hers** — crystal N board jewel, eye with lashes, spark with N at its heart, emerald facets draw an N, N jewel under her portrait; no generic icons on her page.
6. **All the little things** — welcome 80px, statement board larger and lit, jewel pills bigger; the entrance is ten small lifts, not one big fix.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: SN-2350 said the entrance must be memorable — a moment, not a header. This teaching says what the moment is made of: depth. The Real Object Law is the through-line — everything is a real physical object, one light source, real materials, real shadows — and a gauge ring is the law applied to a portrait: the face becomes an object with a dial, a needle, a ring, a depth you can feel. The lesson generalizes past this page: whenever a person is the center of a viewpoint, they sit inside an instrument, not inside a frame — and the instrument moves, the blacks deepen, the icons belong to them. A page that does that reads as a machine built around a person, which is exactly what NayaNET is.

notes.subtitle: **HIS QUESTION 20:36Z:** when they pick a plan in the chooser, what happens on the backend — what does PayPal know, what do we know? **ANSWER GIVEN, plainly:** each block is a Smart Link to ONE PayPal plan. PayPal sees a brand-new subscription and nothing more. PayPal does NOT know they switched — the new subscription isn't linked to the old one, and the old one keeps charging unless it's cancelled. So someone going Power → Max by tapping the Max block ends up with TWO live subscriptions unless the old one is cancelled. **WHAT WE KNOW:** the Smart Link click (which plan was chosen) + the return from PayPal (they came back). **WHAT WE DON'T KNOW:** the payment itself — only click + return, never payment-proven. **CLOSERS, LATER BUILDS:** PayPal webhooks — payment-proven, catches changes made inside PayPal, old subscription ending when new starts — plus the Settings "change your level" button re-opening the chooser. **RELATED:** SN-2339 (PayPal IS the Billing System) — the plan picked IS the charge, we build only the chooser; this note is the sharp edge of that law — the chooser's simplicity has a cost, and the cost is switch-blindness. **STATUS:** the answer was given in chat 20:36Z; the webhooks + Settings change-level button are later builds, not dispatched.

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: **HIS QUESTION 20:36Z:** when they pick a plan in the chooser, what happens on the backend — what does PayPal know, what do we know? **ANSWER GIVEN, plainly:** each block is a Smart Link to ONE PayPal plan. PayPal sees a brand-new subscription and nothing more. PayPal does NOT know they switched — the new subscription isn't linked to the old one, and the old one keeps charging unless it's cancelled. So someone going Power → Max by tapping the Max block ends up with TWO live subscriptions unless the old one is cancelled. **WHAT WE KNOW:** the Smart Link click (which plan was chosen) + the return from PayPal (they came back). **WHAT WE DON'T KNOW:** the payment itself — only click + return, never payment-proven. **CLOSERS, LATER BUILDS:** PayPal webhooks — payment-proven, catches changes made inside PayPal, old subscription ending when new starts — plus the Settings "change your level" button re-opening the chooser. **RELATED:** SN-2339 (PayPal IS the Billing System) — the plan picked IS the charge, we build only the chooser; this note is the sharp edge of that law — the chooser's simplicity has a cost, and the cost is switch-blindness. **STATUS:** the answer was given in chat 20:36Z; the webhooks + Settings change-level button are later builds, not dispatched.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The nine-block chooser is beautifully simple — one button, one template, nine cubes, tap one and you're in PayPal — and the simplicity hides a seam. PayPal's subscription model has no "switch plan" inside a single subscription: each PayPal plan link starts a NEW subscription. So the person who joined on Power and later taps Max has not switched. They have subscribed twice. The old Power subscription keeps charging, month after month, until somebody cancels it — and PayPal will never tell us, because as far as PayPal is concerned there are simply two customers who happen to be the same human. That is a real risk to a real person: double-charged, and the second charge looks like our fault even though it happened inside PayPal's rules. What we can see is narrower than it feels: the Smart Link click tells us which plan they chose, and the PayPal auto-return tells us they came back — but the dashboard must mark it "returned from PayPal," never payment-proven (the 2026-11-05 payments ruling). The honest boundary is the product: we see the intention and the return, not the money. The closers exist and are named — webhooks make the payment visible and catch changes made inside PayPal, including the old subscription ending when the new one starts, and the Settings "change your level" button gives the person one place to change instead of nine places to re-subscribe. They are later builds, deliberately, so the landing ships first — but they are owed, and this note is the receipt for that debt.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you have a ticket to ride the little train every month, and then you decide you want the big train instead. You buy a ticket for the big train — but nobody takes away your little-train ticket! So now you are paying for two trains, and nobody tells you. The people who sell the tickets don't know you switched trains — they just see a new person buying a big-train ticket. We can see which ticket you picked and that you came back, but we can't see the money itself. Later we will build a special bell that rings whenever money really moves, so we always know — and a button in Settings that lets you change trains properly, in one place.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he asked a very good question: when someone changes from one plan to another, what does the payment system actually know? And the honest answer is: it doesn't know they changed at all. Each plan is a brand-new subscription in PayPal's eyes, so the old one keeps charging until someone cancels it — a person could end up paying twice without realising. We can see which plan they tapped and that they came back from PayPal, but we never see the payment itself — we only ever see the click and the return. So the page must never claim a payment is proven when it isn't. The proper fixes are coming later: a webhook that tells us when money really moves and when an old subscription ends, and one button in Settings to change your level in a single place. For now the landing ships with the truth told plainly, and this note is the record of what is owed.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never call a switch a switch — to PayPal it is a brand-new subscription, unlinked to the old, and the old keeps charging until cancelled. I never mark a sale payment-proven on a click and a return — the dashboard says "returned from PayPal" and nothing more, because the payment itself is invisible to us. I never hide the double-subscription risk — a person going Power → Max by tapping Max ends up with two live subscriptions, and that fact is told to him plainly, not buried. And I never let a later build stay unnamed — webhooks (payment-proven, catching changes inside PayPal) and the Settings "change your level" button are the closers, owed and named here.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **A switch is a new subscription, not a switch:** PayPal sees a brand-new subscription; the old one is unlinked and keeps charging unless cancelled.
2. **Double-subscription risk is real:** Power → Max by tapping Max = two live subscriptions until the old is cancelled.
3. **We see click + return only:** the Smart Link click (which plan) + the PayPal auto-return — never the payment itself.
4. **"Returned from PayPal," never payment-proven:** the dashboard marks the return, not a payment (2026-11-05 payments ruling).
5. **Closers are later builds, named and owed:** PayPal webhooks (payment-proven, catches in-PayPal changes, old ends when new starts) + Settings "change your level" button re-opening the chooser.
6. **Related law:** SN-2339 — PayPal IS the billing system, we build only the chooser; this note is its sharp edge.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: SN-2339 made the architecture simple: no billing system to build. This note makes the simplicity honest: the thing we didn't build is the thing that would have known about the switch. Simplicity has a price, and the price here is paid by the citizen — double-charged, silently — unless the closers are built. Naming the debt in the same pass as the answer is the difference between a system that knows its own seam and a system that discovers it from an angry citizen. The webhook is not a feature to schedule someday; it is the proof that a sale happened, and a billing system that cannot prove a sale is a billing system in name only. Until it lands, every presentation of the chooser carries the honest boundary with it: click + return, never payment-proven.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He called it a little detail, and then explained why it isn't one. The chart defaults to Free, and a default is not neutral — it is the page's first suggestion, the thing lit when a person arrives, and "if it's lit up over free then they'll just go" free. The fix is one word of state: default to Max. Not because everyone buys Max, but because the lit tier is where the head goes, and the head should go to the best of the world first, then walk down the ladder by choice. And the free tier gets the same treatment as everything else on this page — a name, not a bare word. "Free" on its own says nothing about what is free; "Naya Free" says what they are getting, and then the thought completes itself in their head: "oh it's nice free, but then I can have Power, Pro, or Max." The free tier becomes the doorway with the house's name on it, and the three paid tiers stand right behind it, named and waiting. That is the whole psychology in one sentence of his: free is the taste, Max is the light, and the ladder is the choice. The dispatch itself carries a small operational note: the rounds 14–17 builder had finished when this brief was sent, so the new builder verifies that work is in place first — the chain of rounds stays one page, not four pages pretending to be one.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a shop with four doors — one free, three that cost money — and when you walk in, the free door is the one with the light on. Of course you go through the free door! He said: put the light on the BEST door, the Max door, when people arrive — so their eyes go there first. And don't just write "free" on the free door — write "Naya Free," so people know WHO is giving them something free, and they think "oh, that's nice — and then I can have Power, or Pro, or Max." The free door is still open. But the light is on the best one.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the chart opens with the free plan lit up, and whatever is lit up when you arrive is where your eyes — and your thoughts — go. He said the light should be on Max when people arrive, because that's the best of it, and then they can choose their way down the ladder themselves. And the free plan shouldn't just say "free" — it should say "Naya Free," so people know what they're getting for free, and then they think, "oh, that's lovely — and then I can have Power, or Pro, or Max." Free is still there, still open. But it's a gift with a name on it now, not just a word, and the light is on the best door.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never let a default suggest the smallest thing — whatever is lit on arrival is where the visitor's head goes, so the lit tier is Max, and Free is the doorway, not the destination. I never leave a tier as a bare adjective — "Free" says nothing about what is free; "Naya Free" names the gift and the giver, and the thought completes itself: nice free, and then Power, Pro, or Max. I never correct his dictation aloud — he said "NIA free" and the name law says N-A-Y-A, so the tier reads "Naya Free" and the record notes the correction once, here. And I never let a new builder start on a page without checking the last builder's work is in place — the rounds stay one page, verified in order, or they drift apart.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **The chart defaults to MAX, not Free** — on load, Max is the selected/lit tier everywhere the selection shows (chart header, level rectangles, chooser, calculator, start flow).
2. **The tier is "Naya Free", never a bare "Free"** — everywhere the tier is named (chart header, level rectangles, chooser, calculator, detail view, start flow, popups).
3. **The psychology, in his words:** if Free is lit they'll just go free; "Naya Free" puts "oh it's nice free, but then I can have Power, Pro, or Max" in their head.
4. **Name-law correction, recorded once:** his dictation said "NIA free"; the name law (SN-2332) is N-A-Y-A, so the tier reads "Naya Free".
5. **The new builder verifies rounds 14–17 first** — the rounds 14–17 build finished before this brief was sent; the chain stays one page.
6. **"A little detail, but it matters"** — a default is a suggestion, and the suggestion is the first thing the visitor's brain believes.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Round 18 is the default law in its smallest form: the state a page opens in is a decision the page makes for the visitor, and a page that opens on Free has decided for them before they have read a word. Defaults are never neutral — they are the first suggestion, the lit thing, the place the head goes — and the most intelligent default is the best of the world, with the free tier standing beside it as a named gift, not a trap and not a bare word. "Naya Free" is also the name law doing its quiet work: a tier called by the house's name is a gift from a house; a tier called "Free" is a price, and a price of zero is the cheapest thought on the page. The next builder who ships a page that opens on its smallest tier, or names a tier with a bare adjective, is making the round-18 mistake — and the check is one question: what is lit when they arrive, and what does it say?

notes.title: One Family in Treatment, Exclusive in Glyph
notes.subtitle: **ROUND 17 — TIER ICONS, ONE FAMILY (queued 20:24Z into builder c469c86f, alongside rounds 14–16; DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — all four header tiers now the same 36px jewel, per-glyph scaling to the same visual mass; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** every tier icon everywhere shares one jewel language — same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar — so the spark, star and crown read as siblings. The defect it names: in the chooser as it stands, Power's spark and Pro's star look like two different icon sets mixed together. One family in treatment, exclusive in glyph — elegant, beautiful, consistent, accurate. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: **ROUND 17 — TIER ICONS, ONE FAMILY (queued 20:24Z into builder c469c86f, alongside rounds 14–16; DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — all four header tiers now the same 36px jewel, per-glyph scaling to the same visual mass; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** every tier icon everywhere shares one jewel language — same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar — so the spark, star and crown read as siblings. The defect it names: in the chooser as it stands, Power's spark and Pro's star look like two different icon sets mixed together. One family in treatment, exclusive in glyph — elegant, beautiful, consistent, accurate. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He looked at the chooser one more time and saw the thing round 16 hadn't named: the icons were each exclusive, yes — Power had its spark, Pro had its star — but they didn't look like they came from the same place. A spark drawn one way and a star drawn another way read as two different icon sets mixed together on one page, and the mix is what broke the feeling: elegant and beautiful and consistent is one feeling, and two sets can't make it. So round 17 refines round 16 without reversing it: the glyphs stay exclusive — spark, star, crown, each tier its own — but the treatment becomes one family. Same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar. The eye should be able to tell, without thinking, that these icons were made together, for this page, in this language. "Accurate" is the last word he used, and it belongs in the rule: a family is not a vibe, it is measurable — same size, same proportions, same grammar — and if the measurements differ, the family is broken, however pretty each icon is alone.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine three little treasures in a box — a spark, a star, a crown — but the spark is made of shiny glass, the star is made of flat paper, and the crown is made of gold. They're all pretty, but they don't look like they belong together — they look like someone collected them from three different shops. He said: make them all from the same beautiful stuff, the same size, the same shiny edges — so they look like brothers and sisters. Different shapes, same family. That's what makes it feel elegant.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the little pictures for each plan are each different, which is right — but they don't look like they belong together. One looks like it came from one set of pictures and another from a different set, and mixed together on the page it just doesn't feel elegant. He said they should feel like one family — all made the same way, the same size, the same shiny jewel style, the same glow around the edges — so the spark, the star and the crown look like sisters. Different shapes, same family. That's what makes the whole thing feel beautiful and consistent and right.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never let exclusive become unrelated — each tier keeps its own glyph, but the glyphs must read as siblings, because a page whose icons look like two different sets mixed together has no family, and no family means no elegance. I never judge a family by feeling alone — "accurate" is his word, and accuracy is measurable: same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar; if the measurements differ, the family is broken. And I never treat a refinement as a reversal — round 17 keeps round 16's law whole (one good icon, used everywhere) and adds the second half (one treatment, everywhere too), because consistency of identity and consistency of treatment are two halves of the same rule.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Refinement of round 16, not a reversal** — each tier keeps its own exclusive glyph (Free spark, Power spark, Pro star, Max crown); the glyphs do not change.
2. **One jewel language for all of them** — same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar.
3. **The defect it names:** Power's spark and Pro's star in the chooser look like two different icon sets mixed together.
4. **The standard is four words, his:** elegant, beautiful, consistent, accurate — and "accurate" makes it measurable, not a vibe.
5. **One family in treatment, exclusive in glyph** — the two halves of the rule, together.
6. **Rides the same build** — queued into c469c86f with rounds 14–16; presented when it lands.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Round 17 is the second half of the identity law, and without it round 16 is only half a fix: a page can have one canonical icon per tier and still look incoherent, if the icons were drawn in different languages. The eye reads treatment before it reads glyph — size, weight, glow, rim — and when those differ, the icons feel like strangers sharing a page, however distinct their shapes are. The rule travels everywhere the icon rule travels: any set of marks that must read as a family — tier icons, benefit jewels, gauge orbs, tab icons — must share one treatment, measured the same way. And the word "accurate" is the check: a family claim that can't be measured in size, proportion and grammar is a wish, not a rule. The next builder who draws a fresh icon in a fresh style for a page that already has a jewel language is making the round-17 mistake, and the audit — "same jewel, same size, same rim-and-glow?" — is the check that catches it before his eye has to.

notes.title: One Good Icon, Used Everywhere
notes.subtitle: **ROUND 16 — TIER-ICON CONSISTENCY (queued 20:23Z into builder c469c86f, alongside rounds 14–15; DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — the calculator's shared diamond dot and the popup levels now carry the canonical jewels; header, level rectangles, chooser blocks and detail header were already canonical; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** the top's four icons are canonical — Free spark teal, Power spark blue, Pro star purple, Max crown gold. Use those same icons, same glyph, same color, in EVERY tier appearance: chart header, level rectangles, all nine chooser blocks, calculator controls, detail-view header. Audit every spot; swap in the canonical icon where it differs. No redesign of the icons themselves — consistency, not reinvention. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: **ROUND 16 — TIER-ICON CONSISTENCY (queued 20:23Z into builder c469c86f, alongside rounds 14–15; DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — the calculator's shared diamond dot and the popup levels now carry the canonical jewels; header, level rectangles, chooser blocks and detail header were already canonical; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** the top's four icons are canonical — Free spark teal, Power spark blue, Pro star purple, Max crown gold. Use those same icons, same glyph, same color, in EVERY tier appearance: chart header, level rectangles, all nine chooser blocks, calculator controls, detail-view header. Audit every spot; swap in the canonical icon where it differs. No redesign of the icons themselves — consistency, not reinvention. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He could see the good work — he said so himself, "you did" — and he could see where it stopped. At the top of the page, each tier has its own exclusive icon: Free a teal spark, Power a blue spark, Pro a purple star, Max a gold crown — a little different from each other, each one looking a little more valuable, exactly the way a tier should feel. And then, everywhere else on the page, the same tiers wore different icons, or the same icon as each other, as if the top had never happened. His correction is not "make better icons" — the icons are already good. It is "use these ones again": the top's four are canonical, and canonical means everywhere — the chart header, the level rectangles, the nine chooser blocks, the calculator controls, the detail-view header. Same glyph, same color, every appearance. The sentence he repeated is the law itself, and it is worth quoting whole because it is the whole rule: "if that's what you're going to use then that's what you use. Everywhere." A good icon used once is a decoration. A good icon used everywhere is an identity — and identity is what lets the eye know which tier it is looking at without reading a word. That is the same law as round 14's colors, in a different object: the thing IS its mark, and the mark does not change from room to room.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine four little treasures — a teal spark, a blue spark, a purple star, a gold crown — one for each kind of plan, sitting at the top of the page where everyone can see them. They're beautiful. But then on the rest of the page, the same plans wear different treasures, or all wear the same one, as if someone forgot which treasure belongs to which plan. He said: no — those four at the top are THE treasures. Use those ones again, everywhere, every single time. Don't make new ones. Don't mix them up. The same spark, the same star, the same crown, wherever that plan shows up.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the top of the page already has the right little pictures — a teal spark, a blue spark, a purple star, a gold crown, one for each plan, each one a little different and looking a little more special. But further down the page, the same plans wear different pictures, as if the top had never happened. He said: use those ones again. The ones at the top are the ones — the same picture, the same color, everywhere that plan appears: in the chart, in the chooser, in the calculator, everywhere. If that's what you're going to use, then that's what you use. Everywhere. A good picture used once is just decoration; used everywhere, it becomes how you recognize the thing at a glance.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never invent a second icon for a thing that already has a good one — the top's four icons are canonical, and canonical means the same glyph, same color, in every appearance; a re-invention is a betrayal of the identity the page already built. I never let a tier wear one mark at the top and another below — if the eye learns "Max is the gold crown" in one room and finds a different mark in the next, the learning is wasted and the page has lied about what Max looks like. And I remember his sentence whole, because it is the law: "if that's what you're going to use then that's what you use. Everywhere." — consistency is not a preference, it is the rule that turns a decoration into an identity.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Four canonical tier icons, named:** Free spark teal · Power spark blue · Pro star purple · Max crown gold.
2. **Same glyph, same color, EVERYWHERE** — chart header, level rectangles, all nine chooser blocks, calculator controls, detail-view header; audit every spot, swap where it differs.
3. **No redesign of the icons themselves** — consistency, not reinvention; the good ones already exist.
4. **The law, verbatim:** "if that's what you're going to use then that's what you use. Everywhere."
5. **Exclusive, not shared** — each tier its own icon, a little different, more valuable-looking; never all the same icon.
6. **This is round 14's law in a different object** — the tier IS its mark, the way a period IS its color; the mark does not change from room to room.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Round 16 is the harvest law applied to icons: the page already had the answer, at the top, and the failure was that the answer didn't travel. Every re-invented icon is a small tax on the reader's recognition — each new mark forces the eye to re-learn what a tier looks like, and a page that makes the eye re-learn in every section is a page that never lets recognition become instant. The canonical-icon rule is also the cheapest fix in design: no new drawing, no new decision, just an audit and a swap. And it compounds with round 14 — color says which period, icon says which tier, and together they let the chooser be read at a glance, with no thinking at all. The next builder who draws a fresh icon for a tier that already has one is making the round-16 mistake, and the audit — "is this the canonical icon, same glyph, same color?" — is the check that catches it before his eye has to.
