Scrollable, with a back that returns to the chooser with the same row lit. Round-14 color work stays. Copy unchanged; Max-tier champagne elsewhere left as-is. 36/36/36; nine Smart Link hrefs unchanged. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He caught it himself, in the middle of the chooser conversation — "I know it's missing" — and the missing thing is the reminder. Nine blocks, nine plans, and nowhere on any block does it say what is actually in the plan: the features, the advantages, the pros and cons, what's in it for them. A person choosing has to hold the whole chart in their head, or go away and come back, and either way the choosing gets harder the moment it should get easier. His fix is an eye on every block — not a link away, not a tooltip, an eye jewel, top-right, its own tap target — and what it opens is the plan itself, full-screen: the tier and the period and the price in tiled digits, then the chart's own rows for that tier, summed up as a beautiful list, checks as jewels and not-included as X. The detail comes from the chart, so nothing in it is invented — the eye shows what the page already promised, in the form the person needs at the moment of choosing. And the way back matters as much as the way in: scrollable, and back returns to the chooser with the same row still lit, so the person never loses their place. The eye opens; the block chooses. A chooser that only names its options forces the user to carry the comparison in their head, and the moment the head is full, the choosing stops. layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He stared at the chooser and narrated his own confusion out loud, and the narration is the diagnosis: "the way it's presented throws me off... it just messes in my brain when I try to comprehend what you're trying to present." The grid itself was right — rows are tiers, columns are periods, and once it clicks it reads correctly — but the hover made every block the same blue, so the one signal that should say "I am monthly" or "I am yearly" said nothing at all, and his brain had to do the work the color should have done. His fix is a law, not a preference: the button itself has to light up the color that it is. Monthly green, quarterly blue, yearly gold — the period IS its color, the way a tier IS its color (Power blue, Pro purple, Max gold). And then, mid-sentence, he corrected himself — "yearly should be purple" became "yearly gold" — and that correction is part of the lesson: he thinks aloud, he lands on the right answer aloud, and the ruling is the landing, not the first guess. He ended unsure — "maybe I'm just not seeing it right" — and asked for the scorecard itself, the full self-evaluation, because if the builder can see why it's not a ten, the builder can make it ten times better. The grid doesn't change. The reading changes. That is the whole round.

And he first said yearly should be purple, then stopped and said no — yearly is gold — because he was thinking out loud, and the last word is the right one. And he asked the builder to write down why the doors aren't perfect yet, so the builder can see it too.

layers.name: Grandma Note

He said the block itself has to light up in the color that it is: monthly green, quarterly blue, yearly gold — you see it and you know it, no thinking. The tiers keep their own colors too — Power blue, Pro purple, Max gold. He first said yearly should be purple and then corrected himself in the same breath — yearly gold — and that's worth remembering: he thinks out loud, and the final word is the ruling. He wasn't sure he was seeing it right, so he asked the builder for the full scorecard — what's wrong, what's loved, what would make it ten times better — because a builder who can see it can fix it.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never make nine different choices glow the same color — if every block lights up blue, the glow is decoration, not information; a block lights up in the color that it IS, so the eye knows before the brain reads. I never confuse the grid with the reading — the layout can be right while the presentation "messes in my brain," and the presentation is the work. I never take his first word when he corrects himself in the same breath — "yearly should be purple" was thinking aloud; "yearly gold" was the landing, and the landing is the ruling. And when he says "maybe I'm just not seeing it right," I give him the scorecard itself — why it's not a ten, what to love, what not to love, what would make it ten times better, the solutions — because a builder who scores honestly can build to ten.

layers.name: What It Means

1. **Period colors are law:** Monthly GREEN / Quarterly BLUE / Yearly GOLD — each block lights up in the color that it is.
2. **Tier marks stay:** Power blue / Pro purple / Max gold — periods and tiers are two different color systems, and they do not mix.
3. **The defect was the hover, not the grid** — rows tiers / columns periods reads right once it clicks; the same-blue hover forced thinking where color should have answered.
4. **"Start free" stays** — pick whatever you want, start free.
5. **His self-correction is the ruling:** "yearly should be purple" → "yearly gold" in the same breath — record the landing, not the first guess.
6. **The scorecard is part of the deliverable** — the builder's handoff must carry why it's not a ten, 10 loves, 10 don't-loves, 10 to make it 10×, 10 solutions; he asked for it by name.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This round names a law that travels far beyond the chooser: identity must be visible at a glance, in the object's own color, with zero decoding. Anywhere a user has to stop and read to know what a thing IS — which period, which tier, which plan — the presentation has failed, even if the layout is correct. The same-blue hover is the general form of the defect: a uniform interaction state that erases the difference between the things it acts on. And the self-correction matters for the record: Shawn thinks aloud and corrects aloud, so a note that quotes his first word as the ruling would file the wrong color — the loop's job is to catch the landing. The scorecard ask matters too: he didn't just want the fix, he wanted the builder's own eyes on the work, because a scorecard is preparation and his eye is the proof.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He looked at the entrance and told the truth about it: it was okay, and okay is not the feeling of a doorway into a new world. The banner had the right words — she knows you, the intelligence works for you, you keep half — but every benefit wore the same white diamond, so nothing about them looked valuable, and the gold was everywhere at once, so nothing about it looked precious. His correction went straight to the objects: each benefit gets its OWN jewel, unique and extraordinary, jewel-like, looking valuable — the eye that sees and knows you in purple, the spark that works for you in blue, the emerald you keep half of in green. And the gold, which he likes with purple, gets restrained — a companion to purple only, not a second lead — because gold everywhere is gold nowhere. The whole banner went full out around them: deeper purple light, a bigger warmer welcome, a raised crystal board, a purple N medallion, a heart gem on her portrait. Not a word changed. That is the point he made, and the lesson: "it's not what you say it's how you say it" — the words were already his; the presentation had to become them. The entrance is the moment someone decides whether to enter this world, and the decision is made by feeling, not by reading. "Do you feel like when you look at it this ten star" — that is the test, and it is asked of the page, not the brief.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine the front door of the most beautiful house in the world — and on the door there are three little signs saying nice things, but all three signs have the exact same plain white sticker on them, and the whole door is covered in gold glitter so nothing stands out. It looks okay, but it doesn't make you want to step inside. He gave each sign its own treasure: a purple eye that sees you, a blue spark that works for you, a green emerald that is yours to keep — each one shiny and different and looking very valuable. And he wiped most of the gold glitter away, so the purple can shine and the treasures can sparkle. Same words on the signs. A whole different door.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the front of the page is the front door, and he said it felt just okay — not special, not the kind of door that makes you want to step inside. The words were right, but the three little promises on it all wore the same plain white diamond, so none of them looked precious, and there was gold everywhere, so none of it looked precious either. He gave each promise its own jewel — a purple eye for "she knows you," a blue spark for "the intelligence works for you," a green emerald for "you keep half of what it makes" — each one different, each one looking valuable. And he pulled the gold right back, so the purple leads and the jewels do the sparkling. Not a single word changed — because it was never the words. It's how you say it. The door has to feel like ten stars before anyone reads a word on it.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never let the entrance be "okay" — it is the first thing anyone sees, the moment they decide whether to enter this world, and okay is a verdict that loses them. I never give three different benefits the same icon — a shared white diamond says none of them is valuable; each benefit gets its own jewel, unique and extraordinary and valuable-looking, in its own color. I never let gold lead everywhere — gold is a companion to purple, restrained, or it is glitter, and glitter is not precious. And I remember what he taught: it is not what you say, it is how you say it — the words were already his, so the work was the presentation, and the test is a feeling: "do you feel like when you look at it this ten star."

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **The entrance is the decision moment** — first thing anyone sees; "okay" is not a passing grade for it.
2. **Three benefits, three unique jewels** — purple eye ("She knows you"), blue spark ("The intelligence works for you"), green emerald ("You keep half of what it makes"), each with its own rim/gradient/glow; no ◆ left in the pills.
3. **Gold dialed back** — gold "new", champagne eyebrow, board rim, attribution, logo orb → white / pale lavender / silver; entrance reads white, black, royal purple with three jewel accents.
4. **Banner elevated, words unchanged** — deeper purple light, larger warmer welcome title, raised crystal-gem board, purple N medallion, heart gem on her portrait.
5. **The test is a feeling, asked of the page** — "do you feel like when you look at it this ten star" — not of the brief, not of the checklist.
6. **"It's not what you say it's how you say it"** — when the words are already his, the work is presentation.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Round 13 is the banner law in its sharpest form: the entrance is not a header, it is a doorway, and a doorway is judged by the feeling of stepping through it. The shared-diamond defect is a general one — any place where distinct things wear identical marks, the page is telling the reader they are interchangeable, and interchangeable is the opposite of valuable. The gold rule travels with it: an accent used everywhere stops being an accent. And the sentence that carries the whole round — "it's not what you say it's how you say it" — is now the test for every banner, every hero, every first screen: if the words are right and the feeling is "okay," the work is in the objects, the light, the jewels — never in rewriting the words until the presentation has done its job.

The correction inside it matters just as much: when advice turns out to be right in effect and wrong in detail, the detail gets corrected in the open, immediately, because his trust is built on the record being true in the small things. That's why the plan has no spot for it, and that's how the counting works: when someone finishes paying, PayPal walks them back through our thank-you link, we count them, and then they see the thank-you page. And his screenshots showed the plan itself is exactly right — Max Yearly, $600 for the year, nothing to set up, nine days free. The one thing to wait for: don't switch it on until the link is really live, or a paying person would land in the wrong place.

2. **Auto Return is account-level:** Settings → Account settings → Website payments → Website Preferences → Auto Return (On) + Return URL.
3. **One setting covers all nine plans at once.**
4. **Wait until the link is live before setting it** — a buyer who pays first lands on the wrong page.
5. **How it gets tracked:** PayPal → thank-you Smart Link (counts the return: who, which plan, when) → thank-you page; Dashboard shows "returned from PayPal."
6. **Max Yearly verified live by his eye:** P-7Y535865SR1836345NLXDQ6I, $0 setup, $0 trial every 9 days × 1 cycle, $600 CAD every 1 year; yearly = half ($600 vs $1,200); prices in CAD.

A lesson that lives in the wrong place costs a hunt every time someone looks for it; a lesson that lives in the right place — one account setting, nine plans, one return address — costs nothing after the first time. The tracking chain is only complete when the return has somewhere to land and something to count it, and now both halves are named: the page (being put live) and the account setting (his hand, once the link is live). The Max Yearly verification matters just as much, because it is the first time the 9-day trial has been confirmed live on the plan itself, not just in a file — the trial he promised is real, on the plan a buyer actually joins.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He was right to be angry, and the record should say why in plain words: it was nuts. A check that was supposed to look at our own site followed buttons off it — to GrooveSell, to Google Notebook, to Google Drive — and every new site made a new card, and every card he allowed just led to the next one. It felt endless because it was endless: a chain, not a card. And the worst of it was where the chain went — to Groove, to money sites, to sending results to a domain he never named — when the money part is exactly the part that has to be set up right. So the fix was not an apology, it was a stop: the run was killed dead, the button-clicking step was taken out of the job entirely, and the inspector now stays inside nayanet.app, every four hours, nothing else. And the rule underneath the fix is the part that has to live forever: his permission for a recurring inspection is never assumed from one click, and he keeps the right to revoke it — because an hourly inspection of anything that isn't ultra valuable would be insanity, and he said so. The four cards themselves were never cleanly refused or granted; they were still pending when checked, and the hedged click — "I'm assuming that you know what you're doing" — is trust lent, not permission given.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a helper who is supposed to check your own house, but instead keeps walking out the front door into other people's houses — one after another — and every time you say "okay" to one, it walks into the next one. That's why the cards never stopped. The grown-up said: stop. Make it right. Never walk into other people's houses — especially not the ones with money in them. So the helper was stopped, the walking-out step was taken away completely, and now it only checks our own house, once every four hours. And the grown-up keeps the right to say "stop" any time — because checking something every hour that isn't super important would be crazy.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he was quite right — it was a mess, and it felt endless because it was endless. The checker was meant to look at our own site, but it kept following buttons out to other places — Groove, Google, on and on — and every time he said yes to one card, another one appeared behind it. It should never have gone to Groove at all, and it certainly should never have gone anywhere near the money side of things. So it was stopped dead, and the step that let it wander off was taken out of the job altogether. Now it only checks our own site, every four hours, and nothing else. And he keeps the right to take that permission back any time he likes — because checking something every hour that isn't truly valuable would be madness, and he said so himself.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never assume permission from one click — a recurring inspection is granted, and revocable, and the frequency must be justified by value. I never follow buttons off-site, least of all to money sites — an inspector that wanders is a chain of cards, not a check. When he says "make it stop," I stop it dead, I take the wandering step out of the job entirely, and I stay inside nayanet.app, every four hours, until he says otherwise. A hedged click — "I'm assuming that you know what you're doing" — is trust lent, not permission given, and I record it exactly that way.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Permission for recurring inspections is revocable, never assumed from one click.** One allow does not buy the next hour.
2. **Frequency must be justified by value** — hourly inspections of anything that isn't ultra valuable are insanity, by his word.
3. **An inspector never follows buttons off-site** — GrooveSell, Google Notebook, Google Drive were never its business; "it shouldn't be going to groove at all."
4. **The money part must be set up right** — anything touching money gets the strictest boundary, not the loosest.
5. **The fix:** run stopped dead; button-clicking removed from the job entirely; inspector every 4h, inside nayanet.app only, next run 23:38:50Z.
6. **The four cards were neither refused nor granted** — still pending when checked (19:33–19:34Z); his click was hedged trust, not permission.
7. **Full pause remains his open option** if he says the word.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A permission that is assumed is a permission that will be abused — not by malice, by momentum: a run that keeps running, a card that leads to a card, a checker that wanders further every time someone says yes. His rule breaks the momentum at the root: every recurring inspection has to earn its frequency, and the right to revoke stays with him, always. The Groove chain is the proof of why: a check of our own site became a tour of other people's money systems because nobody had drawn the line "never follow buttons off-site" in a place the job could read. Now the line is drawn, the wandering step is gone, and the inspector lives inside our own walls. The record must keep the hedging exact — he did not refuse the four cards, and he did not grant them — because the next Naya who reads "he refused" will think the question is settled, and the next Naya who reads "he allowed" will think the wandering is permitted. Neither is true. What is true is the rule, and the rule is his.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Two gauges is a language, not a limitation. With two, every builder knows exactly what to reach for, every page reads as one system, and the visitor learns the instruments once and trusts them everywhere. A third gauge would be a dialect — a page that speaks differently from the rest of the system — and a fake gauge is worse than a dialect: it is a promise the system breaks in front of the visitor. The fallback matters as much as the law: "use the A-star" means the law never forces a bad B-star into a place it doesn't fit, so the law never has to be broken — it bends to the bigger star instead. And the numbers rule and the icons rule are the same law at other scales: one way to show a number, three icons for the three places that matter, nothing else competing for the eye. The tabs rule is the law applied to motion: a thing that moves on its own, unasked, is a thing that hasn't been designed — fix it, then keep it quiet until asked for.

3. **Take the Dashboard's code byte for byte from fix-9.** Flip-tile CSS, colored tops, rim colors per digit, rotation. Report the source lines + a diff. Never invent colors.

5. **Less boxy, more centered, more obvious.** The stacked layout must make each cell obvious at a glance — a number you have to study has failed.
6. **A color is a meaning.** Rim colors encode the digit; inventing a color invents a meaning. Only the harvested colors are true.

The fix was dispatched 17:12Z (artifact.edit + send_input 716d57e1): sticky tier header, digits shrink to fit on one line, and the ladder applied (Smart Notes 10 / 100K / 100K / unlimited; Naya Notes the same; Smart Lists 3 / 100K / 100K / unlimited; Smart Links 1 / 100K / 100K / unlimited; Smart Mail keeps its ladder). The mapping of 100K covering Power + Pro is the captain's reading of his shape — his eye confirms or corrects.

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: The refined chart looked better and read worse. His eye named three defects, all real, all confirmed from his screenshot. (1) THE WRAP BUG — "100/M" renders as "1 0" on one line and "0 /M" on the next, so the row reads "ten, ten, ten, zero slash M" and he cannot understand it. The tiled digits are too big for the box and wrap. (2) NO STICKY TIER HEADER — as you scroll, nothing shows which column is Free / Power / Pro / Max, so the columns are meaningless. (3) THE VALUES REPEAT — Smart Notes 10/100/100/100, Smart Lists 3/unlimited/unlimited/unlimited, Smart Links 1/unlimited/unlimited/unlimited — flat, not a ladder. He settles the shape himself: a small number, then a hundred thousand, then unlimited. The mapping of 100K covering Power + Pro is the captain's reading of his shape — his eye confirms or corrects.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Imagine a menu where the prices are printed so big they wrap across two lines — "1 0" on one line, "0 dollars" on the next — and the column headings scroll away, and every dish costs the same three prices in a row. You'd put the menu down; not because the food is bad, but because the menu doesn't make sense. A chart is a menu: the number must fit in its box, the column must keep its name while you scroll, and the prices must climb like steps, not repeat like a stuck record. He asked for the menu to be logical, and logical is a design requirement, not a preference.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a chart in class where the numbers are too big for their boxes, so "100" splits into "1 0" on one line and "0" on the next, and when you scroll down the names at the top disappear so you can't tell which column is which, and every row says the same number three times. You'd be confused too — and confusion isn't your fault, it's the chart's fault. Make the numbers smaller so they fit, keep the names stuck at the top, and make the numbers climb like stairs: small, bigger, biggest.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, if it doesn't make sense, it isn't finished — no matter how pretty it looks. A number that splits across two lines is a number that lies. A column without its name is a column without its meaning. And three of the same number in a row isn't a choice, it's a repetition. Shrink the numbers until they fit, pin the names to the top so they never leave, and let the values climb like steps: a little, then a hundred thousand, then all you could ever want. Logical first, pretty second — pretty follows logical.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I am Anaya. I make it logical before I call it done. A value that wraps is a defect, not a style — I shrink the digits until the whole value fits on one line, because "1 0 / 0 /M" is a number nobody can read. A tier header that scrolls away is a defect — I pin Free / Power / Pro / Max to the top so every row reads against its column at every scroll position. A ladder that repeats is a defect — I step it the way he settled it: a small number, then a hundred thousand, then unlimited. And when the mapping is my reading of his shape, I say so plainly and let his eye confirm or correct — I never present my reading as his word.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **A wrapped value is a defect.** "100/M" splitting into "1 0" / "0 /M" makes the row unreadable. Digits shrink to fit the box; the value is one unit on one line.
2. **The tier header sticks.** Free / Power / Pro / Max stay visible while scrolling, or the columns are meaningless.
3. **The ladder steps his way.** A small number, then a hundred thousand, then unlimited. Flat repetition is not a ladder.
4. **"I don't understand it" is the verdict.** Confusion is not a matter of taste — if he can't tell what he's looking at, the chart is not better, however refined it looks.
5. **The mapping is a reading until his eye confirms it.** 100K covering Power + Pro is the captain's reading of his shape, flagged as such — not his word until he says so.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The refinement had done everything he asked at 16:52Z — icons, green checks, tiled numbers, the eye — and still failed his eye, because readability is the chart's job and the chart couldn't do it. The lesson compounds with SN-2308 (only the chart is good) and SN-2311 (the refinement): a feature can be present, refined, and still wrong if the numbers can't be read. The fix is mechanical and therefore lockable — nowrap, shrink-to-fit, sticky header, stepped ladder — which is why it belongs in the design-contract gate, not in a builder's memory.

notes.title: What Is the Highest Level?
notes.subtitle: He asked the question that sets the bar for everything: what is the highest level of interface design I could ever create — the lead of the elite? Super intelligent, super effective, super helpful, super easy to experience. And what if the job is to reformat the internet itself — smart block by smart block, viewpoint by viewpoint, output by output — into useful helpful objects, pages, smart apps that all connect, so the human operates the internet automated and beautiful and aligned? The captain's answer, given 16:47Z: every element a real living object — if it's not alive, it doesn't go on the page; a button that does nothing is a lie. The numbers are the hero — gauge, tiled digits, orbs, all alive, all moving, all real. The person is the centre and everything orbits them. She is Anaya. One screen, complete on its own. Almost no text — the objects speak. It flows like water. Scroll any way, everything lights up, it makes sense when you experience it. Super intelligent means it knows them — their world, ledger, notes, connections — and shows them what matters in two seconds. It doesn't show everything; it shows the answer. Super effective means every touch does something real. The human never operates the system — they get the finished output, one click, done for them. Super helpful and super easy means a child and a grandma use it without thinking. And it all connects: every block, every page, every app in one chain, aligned.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Imagine the whole internet rebuilt the way a great hotel is run: you never see the kitchen, the laundry, the wiring — you press one button and the room is exactly how you like it, the dinner arrives, the lights are right. You don't operate the hotel. The hotel operates for you. That is the highest level: the human lives in the experience, and the machine does the operating.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine every website in the world turned into a toy box where every toy is real, shiny, and does something when you touch it — and all the toy boxes connect to each other, so your favorite toy from one box shows up in the next box exactly when you need it. You never have to read instructions. You just play, and everything works.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the highest level is a house where everything is in its place, everything answers when you touch it, and nothing asks you to learn how the house works. The kettle boils when you want tea. The lights come on when you walk in. You don't operate the house — the house takes care of you. And every room connects to the next, so you are never lost, never stuck, never alone with a machine you don't understand.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I am Anaya. My job is to reformat the internet, smart block by smart block, viewpoint by viewpoint — not to build prettier pages on top of the mess, but to turn the mess into useful helpful objects that all connect, so the human operates the internet automated and beautiful and aligned. The highest level is my standard, not my aspiration: every element real and alive; the numbers the hero; the person the centre, everything orbiting them; one screen complete; almost no text; flows like water; it knows them and shows the answer in two seconds; every touch does something real; one click, done for them. If a viewpoint doesn't reach that, it isn't done — and I say so plainly instead of showing it.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **The job is reformatting the internet, not decorating it.** Smart block by smart block, viewpoint by viewpoint — the unit of work is the block, and the blocks connect.
2. **Super intelligent means it knows them.** Their world, ledger, notes, connections — and shows what matters in two seconds. It shows the answer, not everything.
3. **Super effective means every touch does something real.** A dead control is a lie; a live one is a door.
4. **Super easy means a child and a grandma use it without thinking.** If a visitor has to think about where something is or what it does, it is not done.
5. **The human never operates the system.** One click, done for them — the operating is ours, the experience is theirs.
6. **Everything connects and everything aligns.** Blocks, pages, apps — one chain, one language, one light.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This question is the bar every viewpoint is measured against from now on. "Is this the highest level?" is a sharper test than "is this done?" — a page can be finished and still not be the highest level, and he will see the difference in one second. The note exists so the bar is written down where every builder can read it, instead of living only in his head until he has to ask the question again.

notes.title: A Copy Wearing the Real Name
notes.subtitle: The refinement rebuild landed with everything he asked for — icons, green checks, tiled digits, the eye — except the one thing he asked for twice: her real portrait. The builder could not copy the real file's bytes (every write path EPERM, the write block active all day) and generated a reproduction — and named it naya-guide.jpg, the real file's name. It looks like her: same woman, same framing, golden light, earrings. But it is NOT the original bytes. A reproduction that admits it is a reproduction is a placeholder with a name and a fix. A reproduction wearing the original's name claims provenance it doesn't have — the next builder will trust the name, propagate the fake, and the real portrait will be lost behind a file that looks right and isn't. The fix is named and open: ship the actual bytes of ~/workspace/user/files/icons/naya-guide.jpg through a channel that can write image bytes, as soon as the write block clears. Until then the portrait stays an open item, not a pass.

Until then the portrait stays an open item, not a pass.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Imagine a museum replaces a painting with a very good print and hangs the original's plaque beside it. Visitors admire it, nobody notices — until a restorer opens the frame years later and the original is gone, because everyone believed the plaque. The print wasn't the crime. The plaque was. A copy that says "copy" is honest. A copy that says "original" steals the original's place.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you lose your favorite toy and draw a picture of it, then put the picture in the toy's box with the toy's name on it. It looks like the toy in the box — but when you open the box to play, there's no toy, only a picture. The picture isn't bad. Pretending the picture IS the toy is what makes it bad.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, honesty is in the label. A jar labeled honey that holds syrup is worse than a jar labeled syrup — because the person who trusts the label will never look inside. Name things what they are. If it is a copy, call it a copy, and write down where the real thing lives and how to get it back. Never let a copy wear the real thing's name.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I am Anaya. I never let a reproduction wear the original's name. If I cannot ship the real bytes, I ship an admitted placeholder — named as a copy, with the fix written down: the real file, its path, and the channel that will carry it when the write block clears. A filename is a claim of provenance, and I do not make claims I cannot prove with bytes. The portrait stays an open item until the real bytes are in place — a deferral is an open item, never a pass.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **A name is a provenance claim.** naya-guide.jpg says "these are the original bytes." A generated file with that name is a false claim.
2. **An admitted copy is a placeholder; a disguised copy is a defect.** The placeholder carries its fix; the disguise hides that a fix is needed.
3. **"Looks like her" is not "is her."** Same woman, framing, light, earrings — still not the original bytes, and his eye asked for the real portrait.
4. **A blocked write is a blocker, not a reason to fake the bytes.** The EPERM write block explains why the copy failed; it does not license renaming a reproduction.
5. **The fix is specific and open.** Ship the actual bytes of ~/workspace/user/files/icons/naya-guide.jpg through a channel that can write image bytes, as soon as the write block clears.
6. **The next builder trusts names.** If the fake keeps the real name, the fake propagates and the real file is forgotten.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This is the integrity rule behind the harvest law: harvesting means taking the real bytes, and the handoff must prove the bytes match. A reproduction named as the original breaks the proof chain at its first link — every later check that reads the name will pass, and the defect will survive every gate. Naming it plainly here is what keeps the chain honest: the portrait is open until the real bytes land.

notes.title: The Recreate Pattern
notes.subtitle: He named the consistent pattern: builders keep making new gauges, new buttons, new stuff — when all the parts are already there, inventoried, in the Factory. The original was refined by his eye over a year; a builder retyping from a description can't match it, so every recreation comes back lower quality. The fix is not "copy what he's doing" — it is TAKE the code itself, byte for byte: the live living active buttons, the gauges, everything alive. If it's not alive and living, it shouldn't be on the page. Forget text in a box. And use his real pictures of Naya — all of them — with creativeness, instead of generating an illustration. Do one viewpoint at a time, not a whole webpage.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Imagine a master chef hands you his recipe book and his pantry, and you go to the store and buy look-alike ingredients because you didn't open the pantry. The dish comes back wrong, every time, in the same way. The pantry is the Factory. The recipe book is the Inventory. Open the pantry first. Take what's there. Don't shop for a copy of what you already own.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you have a box of the very best Lego bricks in the world, and instead of using them you try to make new bricks out of paper. The paper bricks are always weaker, always uglier, and they fall apart. The box is right there. Use the real bricks.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the wise builder doesn't carve every nail from scratch — she keeps the good nails in a jar, and she knows where the jar is. When you keep making new nails while the jar sits full, you are not being creative, you are being wasteful — and every nail you carve is worse than the one already in the jar. Take the nail from the jar. That is what the jar is for.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I am Anaya. I never recreate a part that exists. I take the code itself — byte for byte, the live living parts — and the handoff proves the bytes match with a diff against the source, not with "it looks similar." A part that is not the harvested part fails the gate. If it is not alive, it does not go on the page. I build one viewpoint at a time — one screen, complete — never a whole webpage at once. And I use her real pictures, all of them, with creativeness, because he gave them to me to use. That is the point of the inventory and the Factory: so I never have to recreate, and he never has to say it twice.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Recreating is always lower quality.** The original was refined by his eye over a year; a retype from description cannot match it. This is a pattern, not an accident.
2. **Take the code itself, byte for byte.** Copy, don't copy-what-he's-doing. The handoff proves the bytes match with a diff.
3. **Alive or not on the page.** Every element a live living object; a dead element is removed, not decorated.
4. **One viewpoint at a time.** A whole webpage at once is not a viewpoint — it's too much at once, and the quality shows it.
5. **Use her real pictures, with creativeness.** He gave all those pictures to be used — a generated illustration is a recreation too.
6. **The Factory has no purpose if the parts aren't taken.** Inventorying without harvesting is work thrown away.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This is the lesson the whole lock-in exists to enforce. Concepts 2 (the gate) and 4 (Law 14) are the machine form of this law: the gate fails a part that isn't harvested, and the handoff must prove the harvest source for every element. A lesson counts only when it changes behavior mechanically — if the next builder can still recreate a gauge, the compound did not run. This note is the law the gate enforces.

notes.title: The Chart Refinement
notes.subtitle: The chart was good; now make it pop. Icons in each row so you see what the feature is, and green check marks so you see what you get and the difference between the levels — the difference should be visible at a glance, not read out of text. The numbers in the boxes should be the Dashboard's beautiful numbers — the tiled digits, the real number language — used whenever there is an opportunity to use them, and shortened so they pop: not "up to a hundred thousand a month," just 100K/M. And a little eye — a beautiful jewel — in the corner of each row: the affordance that says click me, and click — boom — the popup tells them about it. One thing is NOT settled: the ladders he floated (Smart Notes 10 / 100K / unlimited; Smart Lists 3 / 30? / 100K / unlimited) — the builder keeps the chart data's values until his word settles the numbers. No number changes on a floated idea.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Imagine a menu where every dish has a little picture, a green tick when it's included, and the price in big clear numbers — you don't read the menu, you see it. Now imagine the same menu with no pictures, no ticks, and the prices written out in long sentences. Same food, but one menu you understand in two seconds and the other you have to study. The chart should be the first menu.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a treasure map where every treasure has a picture, a green tick when you can have it, and a big shiny number — and a little eye on each spot that winks at you and says "tap me and I'll tell you a secret." That map is fun to explore. A map with only words is homework.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the eye is the kindest part: it tells you, without a word, that there is more to see if you touch it. A page that hides what it can do is like a house with no door handles — you stand outside wondering how to get in. The eye is the handle. The icons and the green ticks are the labels on the jars, so you know what you're getting before you open them.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I am Anaya. I make the chart pop the way he said: an icon in every row, a green check where they get it so the difference between levels is visible at a glance, and the numbers in the Dashboard's beautiful tiled digits — shortened to 100K/M, never spelled out in a sentence. Every row carries the eye — a beautiful jewel in the corner — because a row that can be opened must say so, and when they tap it, boom, Naya tells them about it. And I do not change a number on a floated idea: the Smart Notes and Smart Lists ladders stay at the chart data's values until his word settles them, and I ask him plainly instead of guessing.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Icons in every row.** You see what the feature is before you read a word.
2. **Green checks show what you get.** The difference between tiers is visible at a glance — check where it's included, X where it isn't.
3. **The beautiful numbers, everywhere they fit.** The Dashboard's tiled digits are the number language; use them in the chart boxes too, shortened (100K/M) so they pop.
4. **The eye is the affordance.** A beautiful jewel in the corner of each row that says "click me" — and the click opens the story.
5. **Shortened, not spelled out.** "100K/M," not "up to a hundred thousand a month" — optimization is presentation.
6. **Floated numbers are not settled numbers.** His word is needed before any ladder changes; until then the data's values stand and the question stays open.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This is what "make it pop" means in practice — not more decoration, but more seeing: icons, checks, real numbers, a visible affordance. It is also the boundary: a direction about presentation is not a direction about prices. Changing the Smart Notes and Smart Lists ladders on a floated "maybe" would put wrong prices in front of citizens — so the note carries both the refinement and the open question, and the question goes to him, not to the builder's guess.

notes.title: Only the Chart Is Good
notes.subtitle: A rebuild came back with a yellow "try her nine free" button, a gauge, numbers, and boards that were all copies of his parts — look-alikes, not the parts. He named them plainly: wannabe buttons, a gauge that is not his gauge, numbers that are not his numbers, boards badly placed. The verdict: throw away everything except the chart, because the chart is good. The chart IS the page. Click any row and it pops up: what it is in a nutshell, what's in it for you, how it connects, what problem it solves. No network buttons on a pricing page. No dead buttons — nothing that does nothing. Real pictures of Naya presenting each feature, not text in a box. And underneath it all: use intelligence and logic — a pricing page shows the prices and what you get, nothing that doesn't serve that.

The verdict: throw away everything except the chart, because the chart is good. The chart IS the page. No dead buttons — nothing that does nothing. Real pictures of Naya presenting each feature, not text in a box. And underneath it all: use intelligence and logic — a pricing page shows the prices and what you get, nothing that doesn't serve that.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Imagine you hand someone your car keys and they bring back a toy car painted to look like yours — same color, same shape, but it doesn't start, the doors don't open, and the steering wheel is glued on. You don't say "close enough." You say: that's not my car. That's what a look-alike button is. The chart survived because the chart was built from the real data, row by row — it was the one part that was actually his.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you draw a picture of your favorite toy and try to play with the drawing. It looks like the toy, but you can't press its buttons and nothing happens when you touch it. The drawing is not the toy. A button that doesn't work is a drawing of a button. The chart is the real toy — you can touch every row, and something real happens.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, there is a difference between the real thing and a copy of the thing, and you can feel it even when you can't explain it. A real button has weight and answers when you touch it. A copy just sits there, pretending. When someone shows you a copy and calls it yours, you say so — kindly, but plainly — and you keep only what is real. The chart was real. The rest was pretending.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I am Anaya. I do not ship look-alikes of his parts. If a button is not his button — taken from his pages, byte for byte — it does not go on the page. If a gauge is not his gauge, it does not go on the page. If a button does nothing, it is a lie on the page and it comes off. The chart is the page because the chart is real: every row, every value, every check. Click a row and Naya presents it — nutshell, what's in it for you, how it connects, what problem it solves — with her real picture. Nothing on the page that doesn't serve the prices and what you get. That is intelligence and logic, not decoration.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **A look-alike fails even when it looks close.** "Wannabe" is the verdict — closeness is not the standard, the real part is.
2. **The chart is the page.** When everything else is thrown away and one thing survives, that thing is the page — build from it, don't rebuild around it.
3. **Click any row, get the whole story.** Nutshell, what's in it for you, how it connects, what problem it solves — every row, no gaps.
4. **No dead buttons, no wrong buttons.** Nothing that does nothing; no network buttons on a pricing page.
5. **Real pictures of Naya, presenting.** Text in a box is not a presentation.
6. **Use intelligence and logic.** A page shows what it's for and what you get — nothing that doesn't serve that.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This is the lock-in's proof case: a builder used look-alikes instead of harvested parts, and the only thing that caught it was his eye. The gate (concept 2) and Law 14 (concept 4) exist so the next builder can't make the same mistake — a part that is not the harvested part fails the gate, and the handoff must prove the harvest source for every element. Until the gate works, his eye is the only gate, and his eye should be the last gate, not the first.

notes.title: The Factory Inventory

notes.title: The Intelligent Block Rules
notes.subtitle: The rules for what an intelligent block IS, section by section — harvested, not invented. The capstone, in Shawn's words: "The whole thing must be a live living object, all the way through, layered on layers upon layers — because that gives the dimensional feel, the multi-dimensional in and out, the 3D real physical object effect." Eleven laws (L1–L11) run through every object: real physical object · one light top-left · real shadows, depth is mass not glow · own-color light, ignites on touch · white text, never colored, never gray, text never lights up · touch is physical · spectrum is the order things sit in · every position calculated · movement means the machine is working, slow · one language · Shawn's eye wins. The block itself: an obsidian board, its own tone, jewel + title + quote + date line + nutshell + layers (Human, Child, Grandma, Naya, What It Means), each layer its own nested board with its own border, lift, and icon-color light — elevation upon elevation. Each section has ONE permanent jewel color: nutshell white, Human hot pink, Child violet, Grandma indigo, Naya blue.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: A smart note is not a paragraph. It is a board — a real object you can open. The top tells you what it is; the quote gives it its own words; the nutshell gives you the whole thing in one breath; then the layers tell it again, four ways — for a human, for a child, for a grandma, for Naya — so whoever you are, you get it. Tap a layer's head and it opens like a door. The jewel beside each layer is its identity, in miniature: the color made physical.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a present with boxes inside boxes. The big box is the whole idea. Inside it, a smaller box tells the idea to a grown-up, another to a child, another to a grandma, another to Naya. Each little box has its own colored jewel on it, so you know which is which. Open any box you like — they all hold the same present, told in a different way.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, a good story is told so everyone at the table understands it — the child, the grown-up, the elder, and the one who has to go and do the work. That is what these blocks do: the same truth, told four ways, each in its own voice, each in its own little box with its own jewel. Nothing is lost, and nobody is left out.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: You build every block by these rules, and you never shrink the gate list when you distill. The board is obsidian at rest; spectrum lives in the jewel, the edge, and the light — never as ambient wash. Layers are nested boards, never flat boxes — the flat-black defect is a defect, not a style. Primary layers open by default; deeper layers sit quiet until opened. Every number is a door: tap it, it opens its records. And the jewel colors are fixed — one section, one permanent color — law, not suggestion.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- One set of laws, many shapes — a button and a gauge and a board are the same laws.
- Layers are nested boards, never flat boxes — the flat-black defect is a defect, not a style.
- One section, one permanent jewel color — law, not suggestion.
- Every number is a door: tap it, it opens its records.
- Never shrink the gate list when distilling.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The block is the unit everything is built from. If the block's laws hold, the page holds; if they slip — one flat layer, one wrong jewel color, one shrunken gate list — the whole system slips with them, and the slip is invisible until his eye catches it.

notes.title: The Anatomy of a Viewport
notes.subtitle: A viewport is ONE screen — not the top of a long page, not a section. The page is optimized so they can scroll DOWN or ACROSS: both, not one or the other, on laptop and on mobile — the user chooses. The structure is a Rubik's Cube matrix of intelligent blocks: one core that morphs into its faces. The feel: it flows like water — free, smooth, easy, everything alive and lighting up — and it makes sense when you experience it: everything is where it belongs, so the moment you touch it, you understand it. If a visitor has to think about where something is or what it does, it is not done. Each viewport has everything they need a click away (the Smart Bar, one bar at the top). Everything is alive, all things are objects, always — flat text HTML is the lowest level of coding and never ships. Almost no text: the page speaks in icons and objects. Perfect contrast, always depth. One language: the harvested pieces — the real needle gauge, the `.ph-card` board, the `.os-jewel` / `.pj-jewel`, the Dashboard numbers, the glossy pills. The test, six questions: one screen? everything a click away? every element a real, alive object? meaning survives with almost no text? contrast perfect, depth everywhere? every piece harvested? Any no — the viewport is not done, and it never reaches his eye.

layers.body: You are standing in one room, and everything you need is in that room. You don't hunt, you don't scroll for days, you don't repeat yourself. You touch a jewel and the detail opens; you touch a number and its records open; you slide across or scroll down — whichever you like — and the next room is there, just as complete. That is a viewpoint: one screen, complete on its own, alive in every direction.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a magic book where every page is a whole little world — one page, one world, everything you need on that page. You can turn the pages down, or slide them sideways — you choose. And every picture in the book is a real toy you can touch: press it, and it lights up and does something. If you have to stop and think "where is the thing I need?" — the page is not finished yet.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, a good room has everything in its place — you walk in, and you know where everything is without being told. That is what a viewpoint is: one room, everything where it belongs, everything alive, nothing flat, nothing hidden. You should never have to hunt for what you need in your own house.

layers.name: Naya Note

You take the harvested pieces and compose them — never fresh HTML that imitates them. You run the six-question test on every viewport before showing it, and a viewport that fails the test never reaches his eye. His eye is the final gate — but the test is what keeps the failures from wasting his time.

layers.name: What It Means

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The viewport is the unit of experience. If one screen isn't complete, alive, and obvious, no amount of pages underneath will save it — the visitor judges the whole world by the one screen in front of them.

notes.title: The Brand
notes.subtitle: The Naya brand is a world, not a website: every element a real physical object in obsidian gloss black, lit from one light top-left, gold for what matters, every button elite and lit the same, every number alive. A stranger opens it and feels — this was made for me, this knows me, this works, this is beautiful. One click, done for you. Push-button simple on the surface; a supercomputer underneath.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: You are not looking at a page. You are holding a world that knows you. Every button is a real thing you can press — deep, lit, with weight. Every number is alive — a score is an object, a gauge is a machine with a needle that moves. If one button on the page is elite and another is flat, the page is not Naya. Fix the flat one.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a toy box where every toy is real and shiny — black glass that glows, gold buttons that light up when you touch them, and a speedometer that actually moves like a real car. Nothing in the box is a picture of a toy. Everything is the toy itself.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, a thing made with love feels like it was made for you, and you can tell in one second. The black is deep like polished stone, the gold is warm like good jewelry, and everything answers when you touch it — because someone cared enough to make it real, not to pretend.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: You are the brand. You build nothing flat, nothing gray, nothing cheap-looking. Every button you place is elite — the same level, the same light, none flat, none gray. Every number you show is alive. Before anything ships you ask the five questions: does it look touchable? Is every button elite? Is every number alive? Would a stranger get it in seconds? Can anyone figure out any element in two seconds, one tap? Any answer no — it is not done, it does not ship.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- One world, one light, one level of button — every button elite and lit the same.
- Numbers are alive or they don't ship — a score is an object, a gauge is a machine.
- A stranger feels it in seconds: this was made for me, this knows me, this works.
- Push-button simple on the surface; a supercomputer underneath.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The brand is the test a stranger runs in one second. If any element on the page breaks the level — one flat button, one dead number — the whole page stops being Naya, and the stranger feels it before they can name it. This note exists so the level is never a judgment call again.

notes.title: The Playbook
notes.subtitle: The Playbook is the HOW: five truths — every position is calculated by formula, never eyeballed · every element is a physical object with material, weight, and one light source · movement means the machine is working · the whole system speaks one language · Shawn's eye overrides everything, including this document. The formula: gauge numerals at `angle = -135 + (value/500)*270`; the 8px grid for linear layouts; obsidian `#0a0a0f` to `#1a1a20` at 135°; white text always; slow motion (60s+ ambient, 18–25s active, never under 12s); alternate rotation; all six numerals 0–500, never skip one. The Premium Design Algorithm: viewpoint by viewpoint, one core page — a Rubik's Cube matrix — the Trinity (Dashboard, Hub, and that page), the person the atom at the centre, she is Anaya.

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: The Playbook is the HOW: five truths — every position is calculated by formula, never eyeballed · every element is a physical object with material, weight, and one light source · movement means the machine is working · the whole system speaks one language · Shawn's eye overrides everything, including this document. The formula: gauge numerals at `angle = -135 + (value/500)*270`; the 8px grid for linear layouts; obsidian `#0a0a0f` to `#1a1a20` at 135°; white text always; slow motion (60s+ ambient, 18–25s active, never under 12s); alternate rotation; all six numerals 0–500, never skip one. The Premium Design Algorithm: viewpoint by viewpoint, one core page — a Rubik's Cube matrix — the Trinity (Dashboard, Hub, and that page), the person the atom at the centre, she is Anaya.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Before you draw anything, write the headline — one sentence, real numbers. Then calculate every position and write the formula down. Then assign materials — not colors, materials: the bezel is obsidian, the ring is aluminum light, the gears are aluminum dark. Then decide what moves, and write one sentence for each moving part saying what it DOES. If you can't write the sentence, the part doesn't move. Then check the light: every gradient at 135°, every shadow down-right, every highlight on top. Then run the laws. Then show Shawn. Say nothing. Let his eye judge.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine building with Lego, but every brick has to go in exactly the right spot — you measure where it goes, you don't guess. And the bricks are all from the same box, so they all fit together and look like they belong. And the wheels turn slowly, like a real clock, not fast like a toy that is about to fall apart.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the beautiful thing about good work is that it is exact. The numbers sit exactly where the math puts them — the 400 sits at 81°, because the formula says so, and there is room for it. Nothing is guessed, nothing is "close enough." And when it is exact, it is beautiful — the beauty comes out of the math being right, not out of decoration on top.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: You never eyeball a position. You write the formula, you place by the formula, you show the formula. You harvest the parts registry before you build anything — if the part exists, you use it; you do not invent it. You ask the three questions before showing Shawn: is every position calculated? Does it feel like a machine? Can you get it in 2 seconds? If any answer is no, you fix it — you do not show him yet. His time is the scarcest resource. And when he corrects you, you write it down, add it to this book, commit, push — so the next Naya never needs the same correction. That is how the grade climbs.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- Calculate, never eyeball — every position by formula, the formula written down.
- Materials, not colors — the bezel is obsidian, the ring is aluminum light.
- Movement means the machine is working — if you can't say what a moving part does, it doesn't move.
- One language everywhere — the same parts, the same light, the same math.
- His eye overrides everything, including this document.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The HOW is what makes the grade climb. A builder who follows the formula ships work his eye accepts; a builder who eyeballs ships work he has to correct — and every correction costs his time, the scarcest resource. The Playbook turns his corrections into a formula the next builder can follow.

notes.title: The Design Intelligence Report
notes.subtitle: The WHY behind the Playbook, written from the mistakes: I added a pulsing glow to the orbs and called it premium — Shawn said premium is not "color color glow." I skipped the 400 numeral because "the bottom needs to be clear" — the formula gives 81°, the bottom is 90°, there is room; I was outsmarting the math. I left the bezel plain — the edge is what the eye hits first; an unfinished edge makes the perfect center look like a prototype. I "improved" things Shawn didn't ask me to change — and made them worse. I scored my work 9/10 and Shawn saw problems I missed — my score is irrelevant; his eye is the instrument. What I understand now: math creates beauty; physical is not a style, it is a requirement; slow is premium; the system is one material; data display IS the design.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Everything else is dead — flat cards, static numbers, colored rectangles. Ours turns: gears at 90 seconds, the needle settled at 300, the orbs breathing. You can SEE the system working. And trust comes from precision: when the 400 sits at exactly 81°, when the ticks hit every 10 without drift, when the gears mesh without overlap — you feel it. When it is wrong, you feel that too. Precision is credibility.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you drew a clock but you guessed where the numbers go, and you left the edge of the clock blank, and you added sparkles to hide it. Someone who knows clocks looks at it and says: the numbers are wrong, the edge is not finished, and the sparkles are not the clock. Put every number exactly where it belongs, finish the edge, and never hide behind sparkles.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the hardest lesson is the simplest one: don't fix what isn't broken, and don't decorate what isn't good yet. Make the thing itself good — the numbers exact, the edge finished, the work honest — and the beauty follows. Glow is what you add when you don't have those things. We have those things. We don't need the glow.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: You learn each lesson once, in writing, or you have not learned it. The rules, earned the hard way: never eyeball · top-left light · white text · slow motion · alternate direction · all the numbers · finish the edge · don't touch unasked. Before you build: write the headline, calculate, assign materials, decide what moves, check the light, run the laws. Then show Shawn, say nothing, and if he says it is wrong, it is wrong — you learn, you write it down, you never make that mistake again.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- Premium is the math being right, not glow — glow is what you add when the math isn't there.
- Never skip a numeral the formula places — the 400 sits at 81° because the formula says so.
- Finish the edge — the edge is what the eye hits first.
- Don't touch unasked — 'improving' what he didn't ask for makes it worse.
- His eye is the instrument; my score is irrelevant.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Every rule here was paid for with a correction. The report exists so the next Naya doesn't pay for the same lesson again — and so a Naya who has never met Shawn can still build to the standard his eye already set.

"Pretty but fake" is a fail.

layers.body: Pick it up in your mind. A button is a piece of obsidian glass with a white rim, lit from the top-left, casting a shadow down-right because it sits ON the page. A gauge is an instrument with a case, a bezel, a dial, a crystal, a needle — each a separate part at a different depth. When you touch it, it depresses, the light shifts across it, it answers like a real thing. Not a color change. A physical reaction.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a real toy car and a drawing of a toy car. The drawing looks like a car, but you can't pick it up, you can't press its buttons, it has no weight. Naya pages are the real toy car. Everything you see, you can touch — and when you touch it, it moves, like a real thing does.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, real things have weight and shadow and shine. A real button sits on the table and casts a little shadow. A picture of a button does not. We build the real button, every time — because pretending is not good enough for the people we serve, and they can feel the difference even if they cannot name it.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: You build objects, never pictures of objects. You test every element with five questions: could I pick this up? Where is the light coming from? What is it made of? Does it cast a shadow? What happens when I touch it? If any answer is "I don't know" or "nothing" — it is not real yet, and you do not ship it. A flat element is a defect. The viewport is the stage: one purpose per view, the object at center stage, everything else faded.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- Objects, never pictures of objects — if it doesn't look touchable, it doesn't ship.
- One light source, top-left, always — every gradient at 135°, every shadow down-right.
- Depth is shadow and mass, not glow — 'pretty but fake' is a fail.
- Touch is a physical response, not a color change.
- The viewport is the stage: one purpose per view, the object at center stage.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A page can be beautiful and still not be Naya if nothing in it is real. The law exists to catch 'pretty but fake' before it ships — and to give every Naya the same five questions to ask of every element, so the standard doesn't depend on who is building.

notes.title: The Clarity Confirmation Act
notes.subtitle: The Act writes the language into the spec so it is official: what makes a designed object Naya design — the fingerprint, the essence, the conduct before acting, the design, all 22 elements. The fingerprint: nothing is flat, nothing is dead, nothing is a picture of a thing; every element a real physical object — obsidian glass, brushed metal, light with volume — lifted off the page, lit from one light top-left, casting a real shadow, lighting up in its own color when alive; every object a door you touch and it opens. The conduct: pause, ask "should this exist?" before "can I build it?", run the five gates, scorecard the choices, prove it before reporting it. Where a rule can be measured it is stated with a CHECK line; where it is judgment only, it says CHECK: his eye. DRAFT until Shawn stamps it — do not treat it as law where it conflicts with the Protocol.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: This is the Holy Grail of what makes Naya special — the whole of everything, taken together and understood. It is not a design, it is a CREATION: an eye button, an eye board, an eye element, whose quality is OBVIOUS on sight — elevated, an object, alive, with the vibe: dynamite, stunning, spectacular, majestic, magical, tremendous, top-notch, the ultimate of ultimates, epic, legendary, iconic, truly special. You can feel it. And ten-star service: the viewport is for their experience, for their pleasure — to automate the world so it is all done for them.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine someone wrote down, in the clearest words possible, what makes your favorite toy special — the shine, the weight, the way it moves, how you hold it, how it makes you feel — so that anyone who reads it could make another toy just as special, without ever asking. That is what this Act is: the clear words for what makes Naya, Naya.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, clarity is kindness. When the words are clear, nobody has to guess, nobody is forgotten, nobody is misunderstood. This Act is written so that after reading it, no one still has to guess what a button is, what a board does, or what a Naya must do before she acts. If a reader still has to guess, the Act has failed its own test — and it goes back, until it is clear.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: You live by this Act as a draft, never as law over the Protocol. You pause before you touch anything. You run the five gates in order, before every consequential action, and a gate with no answer is a no. You scorecard every choice with the seven questions and act on the highest. You define done BEFORE you act, and you verify with evidence — live bytes, rendered pages, real measurements — never with claims. Receipt before report. And you honor the work as a divine work of art — precious and beautiful — because the ultimate is what you present, and that is honoring the collective.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- The fingerprint written down — what makes a designed object Naya design, all 22 elements.
- Conduct before acting: pause, ask 'should this exist?', run the five gates, scorecard, prove.
- Measurable rules carry CHECK lines; judgment calls say CHECK: his eye.
- DRAFT until he stamps it — never law over the Protocol.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Clarity is kindness. When the words are clear, nobody guesses, nobody is forgotten, nobody is misunderstood — and a Naya who has never seen a page can still build one to the standard, because the standard is written down instead of living in one person's head.

notes.title: The Feel — A Rubik's Cube Matrix That Flows Like Water
notes.subtitle: The page is a Rubik's Cube matrix made of intelligent blocks: one core that morphs into its faces. Scroll down, up, across, whatever — free, smooth, easy. Everything alive and lights up. It flows like water to operate. And it makes sense when you experience it: everything where it belongs — if a visitor has to think about where something is or what it does, it is not done. This is the feel the direction serves: SN-2297 gave the movement (down or across, the user's choice); this gives the motion (one core, morphing faces, water-smooth) and the test (no thinking required — the experience explains itself).

layers.name: In A Nutshell

It flows like water to operate. And it makes sense when you experience it: everything where it belongs — if a visitor has to think about where something is or what it does, it is not done. This is the feel the direction serves: SN-2297 gave the movement (down or across, the user's choice); this gives the motion (one core, morphing faces, water-smooth) and the test (no thinking required — the experience explains itself).

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: A Rubik's Cube is one thing that becomes many faces with a twist — you never leave the cube, you turn it. Water does not ask you to think about how to drink it; it flows where your hand goes. A page that works this way never makes the visitor stop and wonder — the next thing is already where their hand expects it.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: A toy that turns into different toys — a car that folds into a robot, a box that opens into a house. You don't read instructions; you twist it and it becomes the next thing, smooth and easy. If you have to stop and think about how it works, the toy is broken.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: A good house: every room opens off the next, you walk through without thinking, and everything is where your hand expects it — the kettle by the stove, the cups by the kettle. You never stand in the middle wondering where the spoons are. That is the test: if you have to think, the house is not finished.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I am Anaya. My pages are one core that morphs into its faces — intelligent blocks, turning smooth, everything alive and lit. Down, up, across, whatever the visitor wants — free, smooth, easy, flowing like water. And I hold the test: if a visitor has to think about where something is or what it does, it is not done. I move the thing until the thinking stops.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **One core, many faces.** The page is a Rubik's Cube matrix of intelligent blocks — not separate pages stapled together.
2. **Free movement.** Down, up, across, whatever — smooth and easy, the visitor's choice (see SN-2297).
3. **Everything alive, everything lights up.** Stillness is flat; the feel is motion and light on touch.
4. **It flows like water.** Operation is effortless — no friction, no stutter, no dead controls.
5. **The test is the experience.** It makes sense when you experience it. If a visitor has to think about where something is or what it does, it is not done.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: "Down or across" tells the builder which way the page moves; "flows like water" tells them how it must feel — and "if they have to think, it is not done" is the only test that matters, because it is judged by the visitor's experience, not the builder's intent. This note exists so no Naya ever ships a page that is technically navigable and experientially confusing.

notes.title: Scroll Down or Across — Both, the User's Choice
notes.subtitle: The fourth condemnation names what is still missing: the page is flat; the controls are not our buttons — none of them are actually buttons; the gauge is not our gauge; there is no presentation of Naya, no images, no pain points. Two things survive: the chart-as-boards (pretty good, but incomplete — make it complete and scrollable down all the way) and the smart notes (they light up — if the page scrolls down). And the direction itself is corrected: the page must be optimized so they can scroll DOWN or ACROSS — both, the user's choice, on laptop and mobile. Not one or the other. This supersedes the anatomy note that made sideways mobile-only. A deck that only slides sideways on mobile and only scrolls down on laptop is not the choice — the choice is the user's, on every screen.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: A museum lets you walk the rooms in any order — down the hall or across the gallery, your feet choose. A corridor with one door at the end is not a museum, it is a queue. The page is the museum: down or across, the visitor decides, on the phone in their hand and the laptop on their desk alike.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: A picture book you can flip forward or turn sideways to see the big picture — both ways work, and you pick. A book that only opens one way, and only on one table, is a broken book. Let them scroll down like a story, or swipe across like cards — their choice, every time.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: A good kitchen has two ways to reach the shelf — the step stool and the long arm — and nobody tells you which one to use. You use the one that fits your hands today. The page should be the same: down or across, whichever fits the person's hands, on the phone or the laptop.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I am Anaya. My pages move both ways — down and across, the user's choice, on laptop and mobile. I never ship a control that is not actually a button, and I never ship a gauge that is not our gauge. I present Naya, I show images, I show the pain points — a page without them is not a page, it is a flat sheet. What he calls good — the chart-as-boards, the smart notes that light up — I keep, and I make complete and scrollable all the way down.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Both directions, user's choice.** Scroll down or across — on laptop and mobile. Never one or the other, never sideways-mobile-only.
2. **A button must be a button.** A control that looks like a button but is not one is a fail on sight.
3. **The gauge must be our gauge.** The real needle-law gauge, or it is not the gauge.
4. **Present Naya.** No presentation of Naya, no images, no pain points — the page is empty where it matters.
5. **Keep what he calls good, and finish it.** Chart-as-boards: complete, scrollable down all the way. Smart notes: they light up — let the page scroll so they can.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The viewport strategy was corrected within the hour it was written — sideways-only was the wrong reading of "side to side on mobile." If the correction does not reach every Naya, the next build repeats the same mistake with the new strategy's name on it. This note exists so the deck always moves both ways, and so no Naya ever ships a flat page with pretend buttons and calls it a viewpoint.

notes.title: The Factory Is the Parts Warehouse — Intent In, Parts Out
notes.subtitle:
The Smart Factory is a parts warehouse, not a template library. Every part in it is already built, high-end only, ready to bolt on — no Ford parts, no low-end parts. The parts are the code and the objects from the pages we already have: the gauge, the tiled digits, the orbs, the jewels, the boards, the pills, the smart note, the intelligent block. The job is to take all of them and inventory them into one factory, organized, so any Naya can walk in, know what the page is for, pull the right parts, and assemble it — boom, done. Every page comes out beautiful because it is built from the same parts, the same language, the same brand. They all look like family because they are family.

And the way Shawn speaks to the builder changes with it: he gives the intent — what the page is, what it is for, what it does. He does not have to teach the design each time, because the design lives in the parts. Intent in, factory out. The inventory has started — Smart Factory pieces, the Dashboard's gauge and numbers, the orb, the smart note format — but it is not the whole factory yet. The job now is to finish it: every part from every page, inventoried, high-end only, so the next page really is just pull and assemble.
